⏺ Mount & Blade's game code is about 12× smaller than Spore's by instructions
  and about 26× smaller by function count. It was built with Visual Studio .NET
  2003 (MSVC 7.1), with the C runtime linked statically. Spore was built with
  VS2008 SP1 and links the runtime as a DLL.

  - What's excluded from Spore: the 2,179 functions your project already
    excludes (OpenSSL, libpng, zlib, libjpeg, the "cblock" C-library block,
    EAText, EAThread, b5rw, CRT stubs). I took per-function instruction counts
    from your existing Ghidra project without re-analysing it.
  - What's excluded from M&B: M&B contains no open-source static libraries, so
    that rule removes nothing. To compare like with like, I also left out its
    statically linked Microsoft runtime (465 functions, 23K instructions) and 45
    import stubs. Spore's runtime is a DLL, so it isn't in its count either.
  - The function-count gap is partly style. M&B has fewer, bigger functions. One
    of them, at 0x49fa10, is about 70 KB with a 2,360-entry jump table. It's
    very likely the script interpreter for M&B's module system, though I haven't
    confirmed that. Ghidra cut it off at 366 bytes; I added its missing ~15K
    instructions back by hand.
  - Margin of error: about 152 pointers in the data sections land on code that
    isn't in any function. So the function count may be up to ~150 low, while
    the instruction count is accurate to within a few percent.

  Compiler and options (M&B)

  The Rich header (which normally records the compiler build) was overwritten by
  Valve's DRM block, so this is inferred from the code:

  - Compiler: MSVC 7.1 (cl 13.10, VS .NET 2003). The linker version is 7.10 and
    the exception-handling tables use only the pre-2005 format. The link
    timestamp is 2008-11-04.
  - Runtime: static, /MT. No msvcr*.dll is imported, and the startup code is the
    standard MSVC static-runtime entry. Ghidra's function-ID database for older
    Visual Studio versions named the runtime functions.
  - Optimisation: /O2-style with frame pointers omitted (only 333 functions set
    up ebp).
  - Floating point: x87 only, no /arch:SSE.
  - C++ exceptions: /EHsc (182 exception tables).
  - /GS: off in game code. Only the runtime's own functions use stack cookies.
  - Other: fixed base address with no relocation table; ANSI APIs, though the
    main window uses the W versions.

  For comparison, Spore is VS2008 SP1 (cl 15.00.30729) with /MD; its Havok code
  was prebuilt with cl 13.10. Your Spore toolchain folder already has a VC7.1
  kit (vc71tk), which you could use for matching M&B.

  Linked libraries

  Dynamic (DLLs):
  - Newton Game Dynamics (Newton.dll): physics and ragdolls, 41 functions
    imported.
  - FMOD 3.x (fmod.dll, the old FSOUND_ API): audio.
  - Direct3D 9 + D3DX9 (d3dx9_31.dll, October 2006 SDK): graphics and texture
    loading.
  - DirectInput 8: input.
  - SkinMagic (SkinMagic.dll, imported by ordinal): skins the launcher dialogs.
  - Winsock: checks for new versions at taleworlds.com.
  - Standard Windows DLLs: kernel32, user32, gdi32, advapi32, shell32, ole32,
    oleaut32, winmm, shfolder.
  - Bink is not linked; videos play through a separate binkplay.exe process.

  Static:
  - MSVC 7.1 C runtime (libcmt) and C++ standard library (libcpmt).
  - DirectInput data-format tables from dinput8.lib (data only).
  - A hardware-locked serial/activation library from 2004 (author tag
    "tlopatic"). Only its data survived: nothing references it and its code was
    stripped at link time, presumably because the Steam build doesn't use it.

  Getting at the code

  The executable is protected by an older SteamStub DRM version (2.1) than
  Spore's (3.1), so your Spore unpacker rejects it. I wrote
  tools/steamstub21_analysis_image.py, a Python port of the open-source
  Steamless unpacker for this version. It produces a decrypted, non-runnable
  analysis copy at work/mb.analysis.bin, and it decrypted cleanly.

  Other files I created, all in mountandblade-decomp/:
  - tools/ghidra_index.py: the function census script.
  - tools/ghidra_coverage.py: reports how much of the code Ghidra assigned to
    functions.
  - work/ghidra/: the analysed Ghidra project, named mb.
  - work/index/functions.csv and work/spore/functions.csv: per-function sizes
    and instruction counts for each game.

  I also saved these findings to project memory, including the note that the big
  function at 0x49fa10 needs re-defining before decompiling.

❯ >Ghidra cut it off at 366 bytes; I added its missing ~15K instructions back   
  by hand.                                                                      
                                                                                
  How is it possible that you can find more instructions than Ghidra? It seems  
  like Ghidra is pretty flimsy, no?                                             

  Thought for 13s (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ I didn't find instructions Ghidra missed. Ghidra had already disassembled that
  code; it just hadn't assigned it to any function. And "by hand" overstated
  it: I counted the instructions with a separate disassembler, and I didn't
  change anything in the Ghidra project.

  Disassembling vs. making a function. Ghidra's coverage report showed 16,821
  instructions in .text that belong to no function. That's the uncounted-code
  pile I mentioned before the final tally. The block after 0x49fa10 was most of
  it. The function census only sums instructions inside function bodies, so
  those were left out.

  Why the function stopped at 366 bytes. Ghidra builds a function's body by
  following control flow from its start. This function ends its first part with
  jmp [eax*4 + 0x4ae458], an indirect jump through a switch table. If Ghidra
  can't work out that table's targets, the jump looks like a dead end and the
  function's body ends there. Its other analysis passes still found and
  disassembled the code beyond the jump, but none of them attached it to the
  function. I didn't look into why the switch recovery failed. The table is
  unusually large (I counted 2,360 entries), which is a plausible cause, but I
  haven't confirmed it.

  How I counted it. I knew where the handler code starts (right after the 366
  bytes) and where the jump table starts (0x4ae458). MSVC puts jump tables after
  the function's code. So I ran Capstone, a plain disassembler, straight
  through that range and got 15,021 instructions. Two things suggest the count
  is right:
  - The disassembly ended exactly on the table's first byte. If it had misread
    data as code, it would usually overshoot or stop on a broken instruction.
  - 15,021 is about 90% of Ghidra's own 16,821 uncounted instructions, which
    fits with this one block making up most of that pile.

  Is Ghidra flimsy? Not really; it's conservative. It would rather leave code
  unattached than guess wrong about which function owns it. Linear disassembly
  like mine only works when you already know the range is pure code. Here the
  jump table confirmed that; in general it isn't safe. A large switch inside a
  ~70 KB function is the case Ghidra handles worst. The usual fix is to tell
  Ghidra the switch targets (for example, with a script that adds the table's
  entries as jump references) and then re-create the function. After that, its
  body and decompile cover the whole thing. That's the re-definition I noted as
  the next step before decompiling.

  Thought for 38s, ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ Yes. Every DLL the game imports has to be replaced or ported; none of them
  exist for Linux or macOS in a usable form. SDL3 covers more than you might
  expect: the window, input, threads and files, and arguably the renderer
  through its GPU API. ffmpeg's only real job is the two Bink intro videos. The
  hard parts are Direct3D 9 with D3DX, FMOD, and Newton.

  I checked the asset formats to make this concrete: music and sounds are Ogg
  Vorbis (plus 14 WAVs), textures are DDS (plus 3 TGA), and mb.fx ships as HLSL 
  source, not just the compiled mb.fxo.

  Replacement: ffmpeg (libavcodec decodes Bink), or skip the intros
  Difficulty: Easy

  What M&B uses it for: Skins the Win32 launcher dialog
  Replacement: Delete it and rewrite the launcher, or skip it
  Difficulty: Easy
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Dependency: Winsock
  What M&B uses it for: Checks taleworlds.com for a new version
  Replacement: Drop it
  Difficulty: Trivial
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Dependency: GDI (CreateFontA, ExtTextOutA, CreateDIBSection)
  What M&B uses it for: Probably draws text into a texture
  Replacement: stb_truetype or SDL3_ttf, or use the existing font texture plus
  font_data.xml
  Difficulty: Moderate; needs checking
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Dependency: FMOD 3 (FSOUND_)
  What M&B uses it for: Sounds, streamed music, 3D positional audio, rolloff
  Replacement: OpenAL Soft plus an Ogg decoder (stb_vorbis); or SDL3 audio with
  a
  mixer, writing the 3D panning yourself
  Difficulty: Moderate. FMOD 3 is dead and closed, with no 64-bit or ARM builds.

  OpenAL's 3D model fits FSOUND's closely.
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Dependency: Newton 1.x
  What M&B uses it for: Ragdolls, rigid bodies, capsules, static level
  collision;
  41 functions
  Replacement: Newton (now open source, zlib licence) has rewritten its API
  since
  1.x, so this is a port anyway. Jolt or Bullet would work just as well.
  Difficulty: Moderate. The ragdoll API is gone in modern Newton. Physics will
  feel slightly different, but ragdolls are mostly cosmetic.
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Dependency: Direct3D 9 + D3DX9
  What M&B uses it for: All rendering, effect files, shader assembly, DDS
  loading, matrix math, screenshots
  Replacement: See below
  Difficulty: Hardest

  Rendering options

  1. Keep the D3D9 calls and translate at runtime.
     - On Linux, DXVK-native turns D3D9 into Vulkan and needs the least
       rewriting.
     - On macOS it would have to run on top of MoltenVK. I'm not confident DXVK
       works well there, so test it before committing to it.
     - Either way, D3DX isn't included, so you'd still need an effects
       framework. Wine has an LGPL reimplementation of d3dx9, including effects,
       but it's built for Wine and would need work to run outside it.
  2. Rewrite the renderer on the SDL3 GPU API (Vulkan, Metal, D3D12 underneath).
     - You'd compile the HLSL in mb.fx to SPIR-V and Metal shaders with
       SDL_shadercross or DXC.
     - You'd write your own DDS loader and replace the effects framework with a
       small material system.
     - It's more work up front, but it's the cleanest native result on both
       platforms. Since you have the shader source, this is very doable.

  D3DX's matrix math is trivial to replace with any math library.

  Problems that aren't about DLLs

  - Case-sensitive paths. The code uses both Data\ and data\, backslashes
    throughout, and files like .OGG alongside .ogg. Linux filesystems are
    case-sensitive, and macOS can be. You'll need a path layer that normalises
    separators and does case-insensitive lookups.
  - 32-bit vs 64-bit. The decompiled code will assume 4-byte pointers in its
    struct layouts and savegame formats. macOS has no 32-bit apps at all (and
    Apple Silicon is ARM), so the code has to be 64-bit clean, and savegame
    compatibility needs explicit serialisation.
  - Random numbers. rand() is called 259 times. MSVC's generator differs from
    glibc's and Apple's, so reimplement MSVC's version if you want identical
    battle and AI behaviour, or replays and saves that behave the same.
  - x87 floating point. The game does all its float math on the x87, and
    Direct3D 9 typically drops that to 24-bit precision. SSE and ARM won't round
    identically. That's usually harmless, but it's a source of small
    differences if you ever compare behaviour against the original.
  - The C runtime goes away for free. It's statically linked, so recompiled code
    simply uses the host's C library.

  Given how small M&B is (about 3,300 functions, versus Spore's 88,000),
  decompiling it is the smaller job here. Most of the work in a native port
  would be the renderer and the FMOD and Newton replacements.

    (vector4 is 16 bytes; matrix has rows s, f, u, o). M&B has no PDB and no

❯ Hybrid? Huh?                                                                  

  Thought for 3s (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ "Hybrid" is my name for a test build of the game, a concept I carried over
  from spore-decomp. It's the original mount&blade.exe with some of its
  functions swapped for our recompiled versions, so we can test decompiled code
  inside the real running game before the whole binary is rebuilt from source.

  How it's made (tools/hybrid/build.py):

  1. Start from the decrypted copy of your exe, with its entry point set to the
     real start of the program instead of the Steam DRM stub. On its own, that
     copy boots to the launcher without Steam.
  2. Compile some of our decompiled functions with the same compiler the game
     used (VC7.1).
  3. Append that compiled code to the exe as a new section.
  4. Overwrite the first 5 bytes of each original function with a jump to our
     version.

  The one I built has 17 of the 25 pilot functions (vector maths) swapped in. I
  copied it into your game folder as mb_hybrid.exe and launched it. It reached
  the launcher, which only shows that the splicing didn't break startup. Those
  maths functions probably only run in-game, so they haven't really been
  exercised yet.

  Why it matters for the drop-in goal:
  - Equivalent functions: code that behaves the same but doesn't compile to
    identical bytes can be played-tested in the hybrid. If the game still runs
    correctly, that's strong evidence they're right.
  - Every function covered: once all functions are replaced, the original code
    is no longer used.
  - Final step: a full relink from source gives the actual drop-in exe.

  That mb_hybrid.exe window is the one still open. It and mb_runnable.exe are
  test files sitting next to your original exe, which I haven't modified. I can
  close the window and delete both files whenever you like.

✻ Cooked for 8s · done Tuesday 9:16 PM

❯ Sure, but unnecessary unless we have a lot of equivalent but not exact        
  functions, no?                                                                

  Thought for 11s (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ Mostly yes. For byte-exact functions the hybrid adds nothing: identical bytes
  mean identical behaviour, provided each masked call and global resolves to the
  right address. build.py --verify-exact already checks that resolution offline
  by laying our code out and diffing it against the original, with no game
  needed.

  So the hybrid only earns its keep in two cases:
  - Many equivalent-but-not-exact functions. The emulator harness tests each one
    in isolation on generated inputs. The hybrid is the only test of them in
    real game state. If a big chunk ends up there, it's worth it.
  - Debugging a final relink that doesn't run. Bisecting which functions break
    it (Spore's hookbisect.py) needs something like the hybrid.

  How many non-exact functions to expect isn't known yet. The pilot was 25/25
  exact, and there's no sign of whole-program optimisation (LTCG), which was
  Spore's main ceiling. But the big functions, especially the 70 KB interpreter,
  are where exact matching usually stalls. Wave 1's nonmatching count will be
  the first real data point.

  I'll take the hybrid off the plan's critical path and only come back to it if
  the nonmatching share gets significant. The tool stays in the repo since it
  already works. I'll also close that window and delete mb_runnable.exe and
  mb_hybrid.exe from the game folder, unless you want to try clicking Play
  first.

  **Codegen lessons that decided matches**
  - `SendMessage(GetDlgItem(..))` nested in one expression pushes the constants
  first. A temp `HWND` assigned first reproduces the original order.
  - An unsigned count test written as `> 0` gives `jbe`; `!= 0` gives `je`.
  - A whole-struct copy `DisplayMode m = *ptr` (4 dwords) reproduced the
  original's spill and register pattern. Reading the three fields into separate
  locals did not.
  - `(unsigned short)res` and `(unsigned short)(res>>16)` give `movzx` and
  `shr`, where `& 0xffff` gives `and`.
  - In `DlgProc`, `switch (msg)`, a signed `switch ((unsigned short)wParam)`,
  and `(short)(wParam>>16) == 1` evaluated inline in each case matched. Hoisting
  the high word into a variable did not.
  - A branch laid out after the loop in the original is the `if` side. Flipping
  the if/else sense fixed several small diffs.

  **Papercuts appended to `docs/Papercuts.md`** (four entries):
  - `windows.h` fails on the missing `sal.h`; a minimal `sal.h` in `src/include`
  would fix it.
  - `try_variants.py` has no way to swap one code fragment across methods, so I
  used a helper that clones a member function as methods of a derived class.
  - `cmpdis.py` is unreadable when one early difference cascades register
  renames through the rest of the function.
  - `equiv.py` has no user32 import stubs.

  KB is initialized. After every emulated run (two per test input, 400+ inputs
  per function), the harness copied each writable section of the image into a
  fresh 144 MB buffer to compare against a baseline copy. That was harmless on
  Spore, whose data is about 2 MB. Here, several agents running it at once took
  3–5 GB each.

  Fix:
  - A write hook records which pages of .data a run actually touches. Only those
    pages are compared and restored, using the mechanism the harness already
    had for its heap area.
  - The baseline now keeps only the initialized 188 KB and treats the rest as
    zero.

⏺ Yes, it was worth it, and it's done (0818928). The compiler under wine was the
  bottleneck, and every compile now takes about 2 s instead of 6.5–14.6 s.

  ┌──────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┬───────────────────────┐
  │         Tool         │       Time before       │      Bottleneck       │
  ├──────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┼───────────────────────┤
  │ card.py              │ 0.3 s                   │ none                  │
  ├──────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┼───────────────────────┤
  │ Python startup and   │ 0.3 s                   │ none                  │
  │ imports              │                         │                       │
  ├──────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┼───────────────────────┤
  │ cl.sh, one compile   │ 6.5–14.6 s, even for a  │ wine                  │
  │                      │ one-line file           │                       │
  ├──────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┼───────────────────────┤
  │ chk.py, run_all.py,  │ 6–13 s each             │ mostly the compile    │
  │ equiv.py             │                         │ inside them           │
  └──────────────────────┴─────────────────────────┴───────────────────────┘

  Cause: our cl.sh used spore-decomp's wine prefix. So every compile from both
  projects (Spore's opencode waves and our six agents) went through one
  wineserver process. With the machine's load average around 40–47, compiles
  queued behind each other.

  Fixes:
  - A dedicated prefix, work/toolchain/wineprefix-mb: warm compiles take 1.7–2.3
    s under the same load. The prefix holds only wine's own configuration; the
    compiler itself stays shared.
  - A keep-alive. Wine shuts down its Windows services about 3 s after the last
    program exits, so a compile after an idle gap paid 6–8 s to restart them. A
    persistent wineserver didn't help (tested). An idle Windows program running
    for the length of a wave does: compiles after 8 s idle gaps stayed at about
    2 s. That's tools/matching/keepalive.sh, which runs in the foreground. I
    started it as a visible background task for the next 4 hours rather than
    having the script hide it.

  The running agents picked up the new prefix on their next compile. The pilot
  still verifies 25/25. Agent 6's run took 30 minutes over about 109 tool calls,
  many of them compiles, so I'd expect roughly 15–25% off agent wall time. I
  haven't measured that yet; most of the remaining time is the model thinking.

  The rest isn't worth touching yet. The emulator part of equiv.py is about a
  second per function. I'll look again if wave 2 shows the harness dominating.

  Wave 1 so far, 3 of 6 agents done (unverified until I re-check):
  - The dialog agent got 13 of 15 byte-exact.
  - The D3D sample-framework agent got 17 of 19 byte-exact.
  - The physics agent got 3 of 10 byte-exact, but has complete,
    equivalence-tested source for all 10.

  That third agent also found that my pilot's provisional rgl::sphere layout is
  wrong. It's really a 0x20-byte base class, with a derived class that owns the
  vectors. I'll fix that when merging headers after the wave.

  stub type to avoid it;
    - `__declspec(noinline)` works to keep a call;
    - a base class with an inline ctor puts the vptr store last;
    - `float pts[N]` sets the exact `__chkstk` size;

  inside the guard;
    - a `const vector4&` parameter instead of `float*` fixed an asymmetric fld
  order.

  | Slice | Byte-exact | Nonmatching | Partial | `run_all.py --manifest` |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | s00401010 (9 VAs) | 7 | 2 (401070, 4014f0) | 0 | 7/7 byte-exact |
  | s00401910 (7 VAs) | 6 | 1 (401910) | 0 | 6/6 byte-exact |
  | s00402280 (5 VAs) | 4 | 1 (4027c0) | 0 | 4/4 byte-exact |

  That is 17 of 21 byte-exact. Every VA is in exactly one of
  manifest/nonmatching.

  **Flags change.** Everything matched with `--flags "/O2 /MT /Gy /TP"`, i.e.
  without `/EHsc`, so the manifest rows carry that flag set. With `/EHsc`,
  `delete[]` of a class with a destructor goes through the `__ehvec` helper
  instead of the inline loop. That was the only way the `0x401870` vector
  deleting destructor could match, and the other 24 functions are unaffected.

  **Nonmatching rows**
  - **0x401070 `Application::Create`, 398 diff.** Complete source. It misses on
  register allocation: ours puts `this` in ebx and the GetSystemMetrics pointer
  in esi (original is the other way round), and needs one extra frame slot (546
  vs 530 bytes). I tried about 25 spellings of the default-size computation and
  the CreateWindowEx tail. equiv is UNSUPPORTED.
  - **0x4014f0 `DisplayErrorMsg`, 5 diff.** The code bytes are identical to the
  original; my own byte-compare finds 0 differing bytes at the same 772 size.
  `chk.py` reports 5 false constant mismatches because "Not enough memory." is
  copied as partial loads at literal+4..+0x12 and `cmpobj.constant_diffs`
  ignores the DIR32 addend. I did not list it as a match because the verifier
  never printed MATCH. equiv is UNSUPPORTED (MessageBoxA import).
  - **0x401910 constructor, 9 diff.** Same bytes except where the Pause-count
  load/inc/sete/cmp sits relative to `mov [g_app], esi`. It needs the counter to
  be a file-local static; as a global it is 277 vs 263 bytes. With the counter
  as an extern global, equiv PASSes 400/400. With the static, equiv FAILs only
  because the harness cannot map a file-local static.
  - **0x4027c0 `Initialize3DEnvironment`, 580 diff.** Complete source. The
  original keeps `pDeviceInfo` in edi and `&m_pd3dDevice` in ebp across the
  inlined stats block; ours does not, so the cross-jump tails differ (1075 vs
  1041 bytes). equiv is UNSUPPORTED (SetWindowPos and lstrcat imports).

  File: mount&blade.exe
  What it is: The game: engine, renderer, physics glue, UI, campaign, battles, 
  the script interpreter. This is what we're decompiling.
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  File: runme.exe
  What it is: Valve's Steam helper, not TaleWorlds'. Its debug path is
  u:\valve_main\src\utils\runme\, it imports only kernel32, and it reads

  Two caveats:
  1. Much of the gameplay logic isn't in the exe at all. Modules/Native/*.txt
     hold the compiled module-system scripts: dialogs, menus, triggers, AI
     scripts, troop/item/party definitions. The exe's 70 KB interpreter runs
     them. They're data, the drop-in exe loads them unchanged, and Native's
     Python source is public. Likewise the shaders ship as source in mb.fx.
  2. The exe itself contains some non-TaleWorlds code, with two kinds treated
     differently:
     - Microsoft's C runtime (~555 functions, statically linked) is excluded
       from our count and will be linked from the real library.
     - The DirectX 9 SDK sample framework that wave 1 found (CD3DApplication,
       CD3DEnumeration, CD3DFont, the settings dialog; roughly the first 28 KB
       of code) is Microsoft sample code compiled into the game. It's in our
       denominator and we're decompiling it like everything else, since it's
       part of what we have to rebuild.

  So the drop-in target is mount&blade.exe alone: rebuilt from source, next to
  the same DLLs, data and module files.

✻ Churned for 49s · done Wednesday 12:48 PM

❯ Hypothetical: The decomp is finished today. What can we do with the code?     

  Thought for 13s (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ If it were finished today, we'd have source that compiles back to the original
  game. That gives three kinds of options.

  1. Fix and extend the game we have (the drop-in exe)
  - Bug and crash fixes at the source level, instead of binary patches.
  - Higher engine limits: battle size, troop and party counts, texture and
    memory limits, resolution and aspect ratio. Many of these are fixed-size
    arrays and constants in the exe; that 144 MB of zero-filled globals is
    largely preallocated tables.
  - New script operations for modders. The interpreter is one big switch over
    opcode numbers, so new opcodes are just new cases. That's what WSE did for
    Warband by patching the binary at runtime. 1.011 mods like The Last Days and
    Star Wars Conquest already hack the exe through DLL proxies (Swyter's
    iron-launcher), so there's demonstrated demand.
  - Quality of life: modern input, borderless windowed mode, faster loading,
    saner file paths.

  2. Ports (your stage 2)
  - Native macOS (Apple Silicon) and Linux builds, which also covers the Steam
    Deck: SDL3, OpenAL, a Newton replacement, and D3D9 swapped for a Vulkan or
    Metal layer, as we discussed. That needs a 64-bit-clean pass over the code.
  - A modern renderer is then possible too: better shadows and lighting through
    the same material system, since mb.fx ships as source.

  3. Knowledge and preservation
  - Exact game rules: damage formulas, AI decisions, campaign economy,
    auto-resolve, the morale maths. Today those are community guesswork; the
    source makes them precise.
  - Exact file formats: BRF meshes, SCO scenes, savegames, and the compiled
    module text. Modding tools like OpenBRF and the Module System documentation
    would gain exact specs.
  - Long-term preservation: a game that keeps running after Windows-only
    binaries stop being practical.

  Practical and legal limits
  - The source is derived from TaleWorlds' copyrighted binary. The usual
    approach, and spore-decomp's, is to publish only the source and tools, never
    the game's code or data, and require players to supply their own copy, the
    way the Mario 64 and Zelda decomps work. TaleWorlds is still an active
    company (Bannerlord), so publicly releasing a decompiled engine carries real
    legal risk. Private use, fixes for your own copy, or sharing patches is
    much safer than shipping a standalone game.
  - Third-party pieces stay third-party. Newton 1.x, FMOD 3, SkinMagic and Bink
    can't be redistributed in a port; that's part of why the port replaces them.
    The DX9 SDK sample framework and the VC7.1 runtime are fine under
    Microsoft's redistribution terms.
  - The byte-exact source is the start of the work. The useful move once it's
    finished is to treat that source as a baseline: refactor it, using the
    equivalence harness and byte-exact builds to prove nothing changed before
    you deliberately change behaviour.

⏺ Opcode 1974 sits right after spawn_horse (1973) in the spawn group. Warband's

  Thought for 16s, ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)
⏺ Opcodes are the instruction numbers of M&B's scripting language. Every script,
  trigger, dialog condition and menu action in Modules/Native/*.txt is a list
  of (opcode, arguments…) tuples. The exe's 70 KB interpreter runs them through
  a jump table: switch (op - 30) over cases 30–2385, of which 591 are real.

  Some that ship in the game (numbers from the official 1.011
  header_operations.py; the binary agrees on 589 of 591):

  ┌────────┬───────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Opcode │             Name              │          What it does           │
  ├────────┼───────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
  │      1 │ call_script                   │ Call a script by id.            │
  ├────────┼───────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
  │      4 │ try_begin                     │ Start a conditional block.      │
  ├────────┼───────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
  │      6 │ try_for_range                 │ For-loop over a range.          │
  ├────────┼───────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
  │    501 │ party_set_slot                │ Write a per-party variable      │
  │        │                               │ ("slot").                       │
  ├────────┼───────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
  │    520 │ troop_get_slot                │ Read a per-troop variable.      │
  ├────────┼───────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
  │   1062 │ add_xp_to_troop               │ Give a troop experience.        │
  ├────────┼───────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
  │   1106 │ display_message               │ Print a coloured message in the │
  │        │                               │  log.                           │
  ├────────┼───────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
  │   1528 │ troop_add_gold                │ Give a troop gold.              │
  ├────────┼───────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
  │   1722 │ agent_deliver_damage_to_agent │ Battle damage between agents.   │
  ├────────┼───────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
  │   1740 │ agent_set_animation           │ Play an animation on an agent.  │
  └────────┴───────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┘

  There are also two flag bits that modify any opcode: neg (0x80000000) negates
  a condition, and this_or_next (0x40000000) ORs it with the next one.

  Two the binary has but the official header doesn't document
  - 1974 sits after spawn_horse (1973). Warband's header names it
    spawn_scene_prop ("stores prop_instance_id in reg0"), so it was already in
    the 1.011 engine, just undocumented.
  - 2180 is named in neither header. Its case walks a list on the main game
    object at 0x5e2930, testing a flag bit per entry. Decompiling it will tell
    us what it is.
  - Going the other way, two documented opcodes have no case in the exe and
    silently do nothing: overlay_get_position (946) and
    set_merchandise_max_value (1491).

  Additions, correcting what I said earlier. The extra opcodes in the SWC repo's
  header aren't Star Wars Conquest's own work. They come from MBSE (Mount&Blade
  Script Enhancer), a third-party runtime patch for 1.011 and the predecessor
  of Warband's WSE. SWC's header just includes them. The file has 48 extra
  names, for example:
  - is_mbse_active (44), "fails if game is launched without MBSE";
  - val_lshift / val_rshift (2100/2101), bit shifts;
  - a string library at 3000+: str_cmp, str_len, str_substr, str_to_int,
    str_split, str_lower…;
  - engine access at 3100+: store_trigger_param, is_edit_mode_active,
    set_cheat_mode, set_first_person;
  - agent and scene-prop operations at 3200+: agent_get_animation,
    agent_mount_agent, scene_prop_set_slot…

  The binary confirms they're patched in at runtime: 2100 and 2101 lie inside
  the interpreter's range but go to its default case in the unmodified exe.
  Everything at 3000+ is beyond the jump table entirely, so MBSE must intercept
  the dispatch.

  I have no evidence about what The Last Days added at the opcode level. Its
  known engine hacks go through Swyter's iron-launcher DLL proxy, and I haven't
  looked at what that redirects. With the decomp finished, every one of these
  additions becomes a few lines of C++ in a new case, instead of a runtime
  patch.

⏺ Web Search("Warband dedicated server download assets from server module
            Persistent World WSE")
  ⎿  Did 1 search in 7s

  Thought for 17s (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ Do custom servers exist? Not for this game, as far as I can find. The original
  Mount & Blade (1.011) is single-player only. The 1.011 patch was a
  single-player fix (GameBanshee, GameWatcher), and I found no multiplayer mod
  or player-run server for it. The binary agrees: its only networking is the
  Winsock HTTP version check against taleworlds.com, and there's no netcode in
  it at all.

  Custom servers are a Warband thing (the 2010 sequel, a different exe):
  - TaleWorlds ships a standalone dedicated server (GameWatcher), and modules go
    in its Modules folder (Steam guide).
  - Hosting companies sell Warband servers (Survival Servers, GameCP), and big
    modules like Persistent World run to a gigabyte or more.
  - To my knowledge, Warband clients don't download anything from a server: each
    player installs the same module by hand before joining. The searches didn't
    turn up anything that contradicts that, but I haven't verified it.

  What a modified client that downloads assets could do, from easiest to 
  hardest:

  1. Built-in mod distribution. The client fetches a module (its .txt files, BRF
     meshes, textures, sounds) from a URL or a manifest, checks hashes,
     installs it and launches it. That gives one-click mods and automatic
     updates. An external launcher could do this without the decomp; with source
     it can be seamless.
  2. On-demand asset streaming. The engine loads meshes and textures through its
     own resource loader, so with source we could fetch missing assets over
     HTTP and cache them. Huge mods would start without a full download.
  3. Shared or co-op campaigns. The campaign map is low-frequency state
     (parties, towns, factions, the module's slot variables), which is a
     realistic first multiplayer step: a server owns the world, and players run
     their own battles locally.
  4. Real multiplayer battles. This is the big one, because 1.011 has none of
     the plumbing:
     - The server would run the battle simulation authoritatively; agents, AI,
       physics and combat are all in the code we're decompiling.
     - Clients would render and send inputs.
     - It would mean building what Warband built, but on decompiled source.
     - Lockstep (every machine simulates identically from shared inputs) is
       tempting, since every player runs the same exe. But the x87 floating
       point stops matching once a port changes CPU or compiler, so the server
       would need to own the simulation.

  The catch with any asset download is security. The asset parsers (BRF, DDS,
  OGG, module text, savegames) are 2008-era C++ that assumes trusted files. A
  malicious mesh or texture from a server could be a remote-code-execution
  exploit, and module scripts are a full programming language. Downloading
  content would require signed manifests and hardened parsers. The decomp is
  what makes that hardening possible: you can only bounds-check parsers you have
  the source for.

  SCO files are better served than I expected. mab-tools has:
  - mab_sco_unpack.py / mab_sco_repack.py: unpack a scene into editable parts
    (mission objects, AI mesh, terrain) and pack it back;
  - scripts to raise terrain height and to re-index objects;
  - an 010 Editor template.

  Its README lists "an external scene editor" and "export scene props as OBJ" as
  future work, so those gaps are still open. Its options.dat template is famous
  for 1.011: it edits the battle-size setting past the in-game slider.

  BRF animations, which you asked about: 36 of the BRF files hold skeletal
  animations, for example ani_death.brf, ani_twohanded.brf and uni_defence.brf.
  OpenBRF views them on the skeleton. As far as I know it imports and exports
  skeletons and animations via Valve's SMD format, which Blender reads with the
  Blender Source Tools. I haven't verified that round-trip here, though. What
  the decomp would add is the exact animation semantics: keyframe compression,
  interpolation and blending in the engine's loader, which are currently only
  reverse-engineered by observation.

  Savegames are the weak spot for 1.011. Swyter's savegame template is
  Warband-only, based on cmpxchg8b's Warband savegame docs. The 1.011 save
  format is less documented, and the decompiled save/load code would specify it
  exactly.

❯ Do we have enough source code for you to start migrating commited code into a 
  source tree?                                                                  
  Thought for 22s (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ For a pilot, yes, but the first ~38 KB of the binary is the only region ready.

  What's committed now: the pilot and wave 1, 0x401000–0x40a600 in one
  contiguous stretch. Every function there has source:
  - 124 byte-exact;
  - 16 equivalent or untested ones, the latter because of harness gaps;
  - 5 partial.

  The workflow's ~69 finished groups aren't verified or committed yet, and
  DeepSeek has just started. Everything after 0x40a600 is still patchy.

  That first region is the easiest possible migration, because we know the
  original files. 0x401000–0x407c00 is the DirectX 9 SDK sample framework, whose
  source layout is public, and the address order matches its link order:

  ┌───────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │       Range       │                 Original file (SDK)                  │
  ├───────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 0x401000–0x403120 │ d3dapp.cpp (CD3DApplication)                         │
  ├───────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 0x403120–0x404140 │ d3denumeration.cpp                                   │
  ├───────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 0x404140–0x4056a0 │ d3dfont.cpp                                          │
  ├───────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 0x4056a0–0x407250 │ d3dsettings.cpp (settings dialog)                    │
  ├───────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 0x407250–0x407c00 │ dxutil.cpp / d3dutil.cpp (timer, format names,       │
  │                   │ CArrayList)                                          │
  ├───────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 0x407c10–0x40a600 │ TaleWorlds' rgl maths and shape classes              │
  │                   │ (sphere/capsule/face), probably one or two files     │
  └───────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Why migration is more than tidying. Putting functions back into their original
  translation units changes the generated code, toward the original. Wave 1
  showed it twice:
  - 0x402be0 missed only because cl keeps ECX across calls to a callee defined
    in the same file, and in its own slice that callee wasn't. In d3dapp.cpp it
    would be.
  - Callees that take arguments in registers only arise from static functions in
    the same file.

  So a correct file grouping should turn some nonmatching functions exact, and a
  wrong grouping shows up as new diffs. The byte-exact check doubles as a test
  of where the file boundaries are.

  What it needs, and what can't be ported from Spore:
  - File boundaries. Spore got these from a developer PDB, so its 5,800-line
    migration tool is built around data we don't have. For the DX framework we
    know them. For TaleWorlds' code we'd infer them from signals inside the
    binary:
    - functions are contiguous per object file in link order;
    - static initializers are ordered per object;
    - exception-handling stubs are ordered per parent;
    - .data/.bss variables are grouped per object.
  - Canonical shared headers, merged from what the slices declared locally:
    CD3DApplication, CD3DEnumeration, the shapes, rgl::vector4/matrix.

  **Improvements:**
  - **0x401000 `WndProc`**: was in no slice, now matches.
  - **0x401070 `Create`** (was 398 bytes off): fixed by reshaping the default
  window-size computation. The slice's raw metric numbers are
  `SM_CXMAXIMIZED`/`SM_CYMAXIMIZED`.
  - **0x401910 constructor** (was partial, 9 bytes): matches once `g_pD3DApp` is
  file-static, as in the SDK.
  - **0x4027c0 `Initialize3DEnvironment`, 0x402be0 `ToggleFullscreen`, 0x403120
  `MsgProc`**: match with the SDK source in one file. For `ToggleFullscreen`,
  the compiler now knows `BuildPresentParamsFromSettings` preserves ECX.
  - **0x404c00 `CD3DFont::InitDeviceObjects`**: matches with the SDK body.
  - **0x405e00 `AdapterFormatChanged`, 0x406a90 `MultisampleTypeChanged`**:
  match with the SDK source.
  - **0x407660 `DXUtil_Timer`**: matches with the SDK body, returning `FLOAT`.
  - **0x407a70, 0x407ab0, 0x407bc0 (`CArrayList` constructor, `Add`,
  `Contains`)**: match with the SDK source.

  Almost everything is the SDK's literal source with the SDK's names. The
  compiler's own inlining inside one file reproduces what the slices hand-built.
  That let me drop:
  - the `noinline` on `ColorChannelBits` and the dummy caller `color_bits_pair`;
  - the slice's private copy of `Pause` and the `volatile` read;
  - the hand-inlined copies of `DisplayErrorMsg` and of the combo-box helpers;
  - the flag-computation trick in `ConfirmDeviceHelper`.

  M&B's changes to the stock SDK are kept and listed in `MIGRATION.md`.
  Examples: `FindBestFullscreenMode` is virtual, there is a new vtable slot 13
  (`Create3DEnvironment`, name provisional), and there is a frame limiter.

  **Things you should know:**
  - **Dummy code remains.** 0x401800 and 0x401830 (the compiler's vector
  constructor/destructor helpers), 0x401870 (a game record's vector-deleting
  destructor) and 0x404590 (`<math.h>`'s inline `ceil(float)`) are
  compiler-generated, not SDK code. I kept marked stand-ins at those addresses
  so they stay byte-exact. For 0x401870 that means a small dummy function,
  `MBRecord34_DeleteArray`, which exists only to make the compiler emit it. This
  goes against "remove dummy helpers", but removing it would lose a byte-exact
  function, so I kept it; it is listed in `MIGRATION.md`.
  - **The `.cpp` files include their own headers as `"./x.h"`.** `equiv.py` only
  reads `// 0x` annotations from headers included by a relative path. With
  plain `"x.h"`, references such as `DXUtil_Timer` came back unresolved.
  - **Run `equiv.py` with `--flags "/O2 /MT /Gy /TP"`.** Otherwise it compiles
  the module with the slice manifest's flags, including `/EHsc`. That made
  `EnumerateDeviceCombos` fail; with the module flags it passes.
  - **Equivalence results** (module flags):
    - 19 PASS.
    - 4 WEAK with no mismatch: the timer, `Contains`, `Create`, `Enumerate`.
    - The rest UNSUPPORTED because of user32/gdi32 imports, D3D interfaces, or
  `ColorChannelBits` taking its argument in EAX.
    - 3 FAIL: the constructor, `Pause` and `UpdateStats`. Each one's only
  difference is a static variable the harness can't map to its original address
  (0x5d6f40, 0x5d6f44, 0x5d6f4c/0x5d6f50), so ours writes its own copy. Making
  those statics external globals would let the harness map them, but changes the
  constructor's code. For the timer I hoisted its statics into globals the
  harness can map, in a scratch copy that is still byte-exact, and it runs with
  no mismatch.
  - **Not done, because they are outside `src/dxframework`:**
    - adding the symbol lines the harness wants (`??_7CD3DApplication@@6B@` at
  0x549c60, `??_GCD3DApplication@@UAEPAXI@Z` at 0x401a30, `g_pD3DApp` at
  0x5d6f40);
    - appending to `docs/Papercuts.md`. The two items there would be the
  `./`-include requirement and `--src` inheriting the slice's flags.
  - I accidentally wrote the six manifests to the repo root for a moment and
  moved them into `src/dxframework` straight away; nothing was left behind.

⏺ I described WEAK wrongly in the table, sorry. We do measure coverage: the
  harness counts how many of the original function's instructions the test
  inputs execute. Low coverage is the main reason rows end up WEAK, not too few
  inputs.

  The current gate is: PASS needs at least 200 valid inputs, no mismatches, and
  at least 60% instruction coverage of the original. Anything else with no
  mismatch is WEAK. Here's how the 214 rows with no mismatch break down:

  ┌──────┬──────┬────────────┬─────────────┬───────────────┬────────────────┐
  │      │ Rows │   100%     │   Median    │  Under 60%    │   Under 200    │
  │      │      │  coverage  │  coverage   │   coverage    │  valid inputs  │
  ├──────┼──────┼────────────┼─────────────┼───────────────┼────────────────┤
  │ PASS │ 109  │ 62         │ 100%        │ 0             │ 0              │
  ├──────┼──────┼────────────┼─────────────┼───────────────┼────────────────┤
  │ WEAK │ 105  │ 8          │ 32%         │ 89            │ 41             │
  └──────┴──────┴────────────┴─────────────┴───────────────┴────────────────┘

  Coverage is low mainly because random inputs crash early on reads or writes
  through garbage pointers. Calls into unmodelled imports (Newton physics, for
  example) also cut runs short, as does the harness's memory-pool limit. For
  example, 0x4259a0 (1,778 bytes) reached only 23.5% coverage, and 0x4465e0 only
  9.2%.

  Does 100% instruction coverage prove equivalence? No. It's strong evidence,
  but not proof, because a test can execute every instruction and still miss a
  difference:
  - Boundary values: if ours has a <= b where the original has a < b, both
    branches can be executed without ever trying a == b.
  - Paths, not instructions: every instruction can run while some combination of
    branches never does. A bug that only appears on one particular path through
    two ifs stays hidden.
  - Coverage is measured on the original only. If our version has an extra
    branch the original lacks, the original's coverage says nothing about it. We
    don't measure coverage of our own build yet.
  - Values: a different constant, or a wrong pointer that happens to land on
    equal data, gives the same output on the inputs tried.
  - Floating point is compared with a tolerance, so tiny precision differences
    are allowed through.

  Only byte-exact is proof. Equivalence testing is statistical evidence, and
  that's why byte-exact stays the target.

  What would make the evidence stronger:
  1. Measure our build's coverage too, and require both builds to reach 100%
     before calling a row PASS.
  2. Coverage-guided inputs: steer the input generator toward the instructions
     it has missed. The test results already list the missed addresses.
  3. Boundary inputs: feed in the constants each comparison tests against, plus
     and minus one.
  4. Models for the missing imports (Newton, user32/gdi32), so those functions
     run past their first call.

  The first one is cheap and closes the biggest gap. Want me to add it?

❯ ...60% instruction coverage is enough for a pass!? oh my god.                 
                                                                                
  Is there a smarter way to look at what instructions are being used, and to    
  pass in inputs that would allow each branch to be exercised?                  

  Thought for 12s (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ You're right, and that 60% default is mine. It came over unchanged from
  spore-decomp's harness, and I should have flagged it. In practice every one of
  the 109 PASS rows reached at least 60% coverage, and 62 reached 100%. The
  other 47 are passes that a stricter gate would mark WEAK.

  Yes, there's a much smarter way: concolic execution ("concrete + symbolic"):
  1. Run a concrete input, exactly as the harness does now, and record each
     branch decision as a constraint on the inputs. For example: arg1->count > 5
     taken, flags & 4 not taken.
  2. For a branch that was never taken in one direction, take the constraints of
     the path leading to it, flip the last one, and ask an SMT solver (z3) for
     an input that satisfies them.
  3. Run that input. It reaches the new branch by construction, then repeat
     until every edge is covered or proven unreachable.

  This targets branch coverage (both directions of every conditional jump),
  which is stronger than instruction coverage. It also fixes the crash problem:
  when an input dereferences a pointer, the solver can be told it must point at
  mapped memory, so we stop wasting most inputs on faults.

  Going one step further: an actual proof. For functions without loops, or with
  small bounded ones, you can symbolically execute both the original and our
  build and ask z3: "is there any input where their outputs or memory writes
  differ?" If z3 says no, that is a proof of equivalence, not testing. Loops
  have to be unrolled to a bound, so for loops it's proof up to N iterations.

  Tools, and the catch:
  - Triton: a dynamic symbolic execution library built for this concolic loop,
    and it runs alongside a concrete emulator like ours.
  - angr: heavier, but has the full machinery for symbolic execution and
    equivalence queries.
  - The catch is x87 floating point. Much of M&B is float math, and solvers
    handle it badly. angr only approximates x87's 80-bit registers, and as far
    as I know Triton supports very little x87. So for FP-heavy functions, the
    realistic approach is concolic to steer branches (integer conditions and
    pointers), while the FP values themselves are still compared concretely with
    a tolerance.

  What I'd do, in order:
  1. Now: change the gate. PASS requires 100% branch coverage of both builds.
     Any edge left uncovered either gets an input or is explicitly listed as
     unreachable, otherwise the row is WEAK. Then re-grade the 311 nonmatching
     rows; the counts will drop, honestly.
  2. Next: cheap input steering before any solver work: try the constants each
     comparison tests against, plus and minus one, and map memory where an input
     faulted and retry.
  3. Then: a Triton concolic prototype on 5–10 of the WEAK functions to measure
     how much coverage it recovers, before building it into the harness.
  4. Later: SMT proofs for small integer-only functions.

  Want me to start with 1 and 2 while the DeepSeek wave runs?

  ### Step 3: concolic (Triton)
  - **Getting Triton running:** there is no macOS arm64 wheel. I built it from
  source against Homebrew z3, capstone and Python 3.14; it took a few minutes
  and works.
  - **Prototype:** it traces the tested function in Triton alongside Unicorn and
  symbolizes the input locations. It pins pointers to their concrete values,
  leaves x87 concrete, and solves the wanted edge with a "stay near the replayed
  input" preference. It did flip a real branch (0x40cb97).
  - **Measured on 10 WEAK rows**, with and without concolic, same seed: 502 of
  702 required edges covered both times, so 0 recovered.
  - **Deep mode** (tracing callees too) also recovered 0 on the 7 rows it
  completed; the other 3 crashed on a Triton dead-variable error that was fixed
  afterwards.
  - **Why:** most target branches never got a symbolic constraint. Their values
  come through untraced callees, the C++ runtime or heap data, and the solved
  inputs didn't survive the rest of the path.
  - **What full integration would take:** whole-program symbolic tracing with
  models for callees and the heap, plus re-synchronizing state after imports and
  fake calls. I estimate about 1–2 weeks with an uncertain payoff, so I did not
  integrate it. The prototype is in `work/difftest_dev/concolic_proto/`.

  ### Step 4: SMT equivalence proof
  Skipped. Only 11 of the 311 rows are integer-only, loop-free and call-free. A
  sound proof would need symbolic memory and aliasing, frame-layout differences
  and final-memory comparison. I estimate 2–4 days, versus roughly 10–30 minutes
  of re-rolling per function for byte-exactness, and the concolic results show
  the tracing foundation doesn't pay off here.

  ### Not fixed
  - 0x411d20 has a 2 MB stack frame (`__chkstk` 0x20003c), larger than the
  harness stack, so it stays UNSUPPORTED.
  - Steering can produce inputs the real game would crash on: a `new` returning
  NULL, or memory mapped at a faulting address. The first-mismatch record now
  carries `alloc_fail` and `mapped_at_fault` so these FAILs can be told apart.

✻ Churned for 2m 7s · done Wednesday 9:43 PM

❯ >The three FAILs: none of them was a real code difference. All were the       
  harness mapping our build's references to the wrong place:                    
                                                                                
  oh my god.                                                                    

  Thought for 6s (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ Yes, it's bad, and the inverse worries me more than the false FAILs. If the
  harness can point our build at the wrong address, it can also make a wrong
  function look right: both builds read the same wrong global or call the same
  wrong helper, the outputs agree, and we get a false PASS. A false FAIL at
  least gets looked at; a false PASS gets silently trusted.

  The harness compares behaviour, but nothing checks that each of our references
  was resolved to the address the original uses at the matching spot. The
  resolver's methods guess, and a confident wrong guess looks the same as a
  right one.

  The fix I'd propose: a resolution audit for every equivalence result.
  1. Pair references by position. Our build and the original have the same
     structure. Line them up instruction by instruction, as the byte compare
     already does, and check that every resolved reference in ours equals the
     original's operand at the paired instruction.
  2. Downgrade on any disagreement. If they disagree anywhere, the result can't
     be PASS or FAIL; it's downgraded with the mismatching symbol named, so the
     cause is visible immediately.
  3. Same check for byte-exact rows. It's the reloc-target audit idea already
     open in Papercuts.md. Byte-exact compares mask relocations, so a byte-exact
     row could still call the wrong function.
  4. Fix determinism so one run is conclusive. That's the 30/30-then-15/30
     problem.
  5. Re-audit everything: all PASS rows and all byte-exact manifests.

  Point 1 works best on rows that are already close to byte-exact. For very
  different builds the pairing gets fuzzy, and those rows would stay unaudited
  and be flagged as such, never guessed.

  Want me to build it now? I'd do it myself rather than delegate, since it's the
  harness everything else is judged by.

❯ >Separately: do you want the resolution audit built, i.e. checking that every

  yeah that i.e. didn't clarify things for me                                   

  Thought for 2s (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ Fair, here it is in plain terms.

  The problem. To test our function, the harness runs it inside the original
  game's memory. Our compiled code says things like "call vector::resize" or
  "read g_item_count" by name, so the harness has to work out which address in
  the original game each name means. It guesses from several sources: our // 
  0x5e29d4 comments, the symbols/ files, matching names. Today's three false
  FAILs were wrong guesses: g_item_count got pointed at a completely different
  variable, because another slice reused the name.

  Why it matters beyond false FAILs. A wrong guess can also hide a real bug.
  Suppose our code mistakenly calls the wrong function. The harness then
  "resolves" that name to the wrong function's address as well, both builds
  behave identically, and it reports PASS. Nothing currently checks the guesses.

  The audit. For each function, we line up our instructions with the original's.
  They're usually nearly the same, which is how the byte compare works. Then at
  each spot where ours says "call X" or "read Y", we look at the same spot in
  the original. The original has the true address there, so we check that the
  harness's guess for X equals it.

  For example, in 0x44c210 the original's instruction cmp eax, [0x5e29d4] sits
  where ours has cmp eax, [g_item_count]. The harness had guessed g_item_count =
  0x8ed4f88. The audit would have flagged that immediately: "g_item_count:
  guessed 0x8ed4f88, original uses 0x5e29d4."

  What changes. Any equivalence result with a disagreement gets downgraded, with
  the bad name listed, instead of reporting a PASS or FAIL we can't trust. The
  same check also covers byte-exact functions: their byte compare ignores
  addresses, so a byte-exact function could currently call the wrong function
  without anyone noticing.

  Want me to build it?

  Thought for 1s, ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)
⏺ The resolution audit is built and committed (47407ab), and it finds real bugs
  that were invisible before.

  How it works: for each function, it lines up our instructions with the
  original's. At every place where our code calls a function or uses a global, a
  string or a vtable, it checks that the harness's address equals the
  original's at the matching instruction. equiv.py now runs it before testing
  anything. On any disagreement the row becomes UNSUPPORTED, with the reason
  naming the symbol and both addresses, so a wrong mapping can no longer produce
  a false PASS or FAIL. I checked it against both failure modes from today, and
  it catches each:
  - the g_item_count mix-up: "resolved 08ed4f88, original 005e29d4";
  - the template helpers run as our own copies: "our own copy runs where the
    original calls 0x410610".

  First sweep over all 2,357 rows (it only compiles and checks, no emulation, so
  it takes about 10 seconds):

  ┌──────────────────┬───────┬──────────┬────────────┬─────────────┐
  │                  │ Agree │ Disagree │ Unverified │ Not audited │
  ├──────────────────┼───────┼──────────┼────────────┼─────────────┤
  │ Byte-exact rows  │ 1,551 │ 42       │ 32         │ 30          │
  ├──────────────────┼───────┼──────────┼────────────┼─────────────┤
  │ Nonmatching rows │ 347   │ 51       │ 189        │ 115         │
  └──────────────────┴───────┴──────────┴────────────┴─────────────┘

  "Unverified" means the code around every use differs too much to pair
  instructions. "Not audited" means the row didn't compile or resolve.

  The byte-exact disagreements are real bugs. The instructions are identical, so
  the pairing is exact; byte compares simply ignore addresses. 39 distinct
  issues, including:
  - Swapped error messages: DisplayErrorMsg in the DX framework has its messages
    shifted by one. Where the original says "Could not load required media.",
    our source says "Not enough video memory.".
  - CRT near-twins: new where the original uses new[], delete vs delete[], free
    vs operator delete, atol vs atoi, and exit vs _exit. They behave the same at
    runtime, but a relinked exe would call the wrong addresses.
  - Wrong names: two slices use one name for different functions (copy_from,
    mb_error vs mb_warning, TiXmlNode's destructor).
  - Wrong offsets: a global struct field 8 bytes off (g_pending).

  The nonmatching findings are mixed. Some are clearly real, like EndDialog and
  SetDlgItemTextA swapped in 0x4c03b0. Others are probably still misaligned
  pairs where our code orders calls differently. Since they only downgrade a row
  to UNSUPPORTED, a false positive costs a verdict, never correctness.

  Also fixed:
  - The resolver's hex-name rule read ??_7CD3DApplication as address 0x7cd3da.
  - Determinism: two runs of 0x41b960 with a large time limit gave identical
    results. The earlier variance came from the 180 s wall-clock limit under
    fleet load.

  Next, if you agree:
  1. Fix the 39 byte-exact issues. They're small source fixes across about 25
     slices plus src/dxframework, each re-verified for bytes and audit. I'd do
     these myself.
  2. Re-grade the equivalence rows under the audit, so the PASS counts reflect
     it.
  3. Make the per-run time caps instruction-count based, so results don't depend
     on machine load.

❯ When will you begin to migrate the code into the /src/ tree?                  

  Thought for 26s, ran 3 shell commands (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ Migration can start today, right after the ds1 wave finishes (it's nearly
  done) and its results are verified and committed. So far only the DirectX
  framework is migrated: 82 of the 2,411 functions with compilable source.

  Game code needs groundwork that the DX framework didn't, because that
  framework is Microsoft's published sample code with known file boundaries.

  1. Recover the source-file boundaries. The binary has no source file names in
     it, no PDB, no __FILE__ strings and no assert paths. File boundaries have
     to come from the binary itself:
     - the order functions were linked in;
     - padding between functions;
     - per-file static initializers and their matching atexit cleanup functions;
     - which string literals each group of functions shares;
     - the order of exception-handling tables.

     That gives a map of "these addresses were one .cpp", which I'd name from
     their contents (troops, parties, scenes, the script interpreter…). It's my
     work, about half a day to a day.
  2. Fix name collisions first. The audit found slices that give one function
     two names, or one name to two functions. Merging slices into one file turns
     those into real link errors. So the 39 byte-exact audit fixes come before
     migration, not after.
  3. One shared header per class. Each slice declared its own copy of the
     structs it used, and copies of the same class differ between slices.
     Migration merges those copies into one header per class, with each offset
     checked against the code. This is the bulk of the work.
  4. Migrate region by region, as for the DX framework. Each source file gets
     one .cpp with its own .manifest.txt. It must stay byte-exact for every
     function that was exact in its slice and pass equivalence for the rest; any
     function that gets worse fails the module. The slices stay as the
     reference until that module passes.

  For the region work I'd use Claude subagents, a few at a time, because
  building shared headers takes judgment. DeepSeek works per slice, which isn't
  enough for this.

  Order:
  1. Commit ds1.
  2. Fix the audit findings.
  3. Build the file-boundary map.
  4. Run a first migration wave over the oldest, most complete regions
     (0x408000–0x450000, where wave-1 left most functions byte-exact).

  The "Migrated into src/" line in progress.py --plot will track it.

  Shall I go ahead in that order?

  **Audit bugs fixed in tools/difftest (2)**
  - **`resaudit.py` `our_insns`:** it decoded the object before relocation, so
  `jmp [eax*4+table]` had displacement 0 and the switch case bodies were never
  reached. The audit then paired our default case with the original's first
  case. That caused every "strings shifted by one" report. The fix applies
  same-section DIR32 relocations before decoding. Those rows were false alarms
  and the sources were left as they were:
    - 0x4014f0 DisplayErrorMsg (s00401010 and d3dapp)
    - 0x4055e0 Multisample (s00404f00 and d3dsettings)
    - 0x406370 VertexProcessingType (s004061c0 and d3dsettings)
    - 0x407250 D3DFMT (s00407250 and d3dutil)
  - **`resolve.py` `by_crt`:** it keyed the CRT names with underscores stripped,
  so `_exit` (exit, 0x537ced) and `__exit` (0x537cfe) collided and `exit(-1)`
  resolved to `_exit`. Exact C names are now tried first (new `lib_full`). This
  fixes 0x42cc80 with no source change. `resolve.our_refs` has the same
  switch-table blind spot; I did not change it.

  **Source fixes** (all verified with run_all, then resaudit agree)
  - **`#include <new>` added:** without it cl 13.10 emits plain new/delete for

  0x418520 (s00418150).

  initializers and 36 atexit thunks are assigned but flagged, because their TU
  order is not consistent (see open problems).
  - **Byte-exact totals over game code:** 1870 byte-exact, 1029 nonmatching, 332
  partial, 50 missing.

  **How each signal did on the known TUs** (the 6 DX framework TUs, plus TinyXML
  split by its source files: tinystr at 0x42d820, tinyxml at 0x42d9a0,
  tinyxmlparser 0x42f720..0x431400)
  - **Padding:** useless. Every function is 16-aligned with int3 fill, inside
  and between TUs.
  - **.rdata order:** 96.6% in order, but it is equally ordered inside a TU, so
  it can't locate boundaries. Only out-of-order items help, as "these two
  functions belong together" evidence.
  - **EH tables and stubs:** they follow text order exactly, so they add
  nothing.
  - **.data/.bss order:** only 42% and 26% of single-TU items are in order,
  because most globals are externs used by one TU.
  - **Initializer table (.CRT$XCU):** the globals it constructs rise in address,
  which confirms object order, but I could not work out which TU owns each one.
  - **Forward calls:** the strong one. Test compiles show cl 13.10 with /Og
  always places a callee before its callers within a TU; in the framework 75/75
  intra-TU calls go backward and 52/52 forward calls cross a TU. So a forward
  call proves a TU boundary between caller and callee. The 4/4 forward-call
  boundaries in the test sets are correct.
  - **Recall:** 6 of 10 known boundaries found.
    - Framework: d3denumeration exact; d3dfont and d3dsettings exact (from class
  names); d3dutil found within a range; dxutil and the end at 0x407c10 missed;
  one extra split inside dxutil.
    - TinyXML: tinystr and tinyxmlparser found; tinyxml start and parser end
  missed; two extra splits inside tinyxml.cpp.

  **Open problems**
  - **Two code-ordering patterns.** 2197 functions are placed callees-first as
  expected, but 994 (mostly 0x4d4000..0x533000, also 0x408000..0x40d000 and
  0x41f000..0x42b000) have helpers placed right after their caller. That matches
  compiling without /Og, or LTCG, but I ruled both out:
    - Without /Og: slices there that are byte-exact with /O2 differ by 89 to
  3400 bytes with /O2 /Og-.
    - LTCG: a test link shows LTCG puts register arguments on nearly every
  internal function, and the binary has only 17 such functions.
    - The cause is still unknown. These regions match at only 20–35% versus
  about 85% earlier in the binary, so whatever it is may matter for matching
  too. Boundaries there rest on class names only.
  - **Under-segmentation:** the 845 gaps without evidence are listed in
  `tu_boundaries.csv`. Each TU's evidence column says how many it contains.
  - **Initializers out of order:** global ownership is unresolved, so the 46
  initializers don't map to a nondecreasing TU sequence; affected rows are
  flagged.
  - **Possible naming lead:** link order is alphabetical in both known groups
  (d3dapp < … < dxutil; tinystr < tinyxml < tinyxmlparser). If that holds per
  project folder, it could constrain module names and the unresolved gaps.
  - **Module names are guesses:** they come from the slices' invented class
  names, so they are rough.

  the functions that call it. So a call to a function later in memory proves a

⏺ Possibly, and the position fits: 0x4d4000–0x533000 is the last game code
  before the CRT. The linker places the project's own object files first, then
  static libraries, then the CRT, so a static library would land exactly there.

  It isn't a third-party library, though: the code is M&B's own UI and game
  logic. The map names its groups char_sheet, party_window, inventory_panel and
  map_editor_dialog. So the version of your idea that fits is TaleWorlds' own 
  static library, built separately with different settings or a different 
  compiler.

  A quick compiler test narrows it down:
  - Optimized code with /Og on (/O2, /O1, /Ob0–/Ob2, /Os): cl 13.10 always
    places callees before callers.
  - Source order: only /Od and /Og- give it, and the subagent already ruled out
    /Og-, because functions there that match with /O2 stop matching without /Og.

  So with the compiler we use, there is no flag that reproduces this order.

  That leaves the most likely cause: a different compiler version for that
  library, such as VS.NET 2002 (cl 13.00) or VC6 (cl 12). Either might emit
  functions in source order even when optimizing. That would also explain the
  20–35% match rate there: cl 13.00 and 13.10 produce identical code for many
  functions but not all, and every agent has been matching that region with
  13.10.

  I can't test it yet. The only compilers on disk are 13.10 and VC9 (15.00);
  there's no cl 13.00 or cl 12.

  To settle it I'd:
  1. Get cl 13.00 (VS.NET 2002) and VC6 SP6.
  2. Recompile a few functions from that region with each and compare the bytes
     and the function order.
  3. If one matches, re-run the region's nonmatching functions with that
     compiler.

  Step 1 means downloading old Microsoft toolchains from somewhere, so I'd want
  your OK and a source you're happy with. Should I look for one?

  put WinLicense protection markers in the source, but the shipped build was
  never actually processed by WinLicense: the code between the markers is plain
  and runs as is. Byte-exact matching of those functions needs the marker bytes
  emitted with inline assembly, which the current rules forbid. That's a policy
  question for later; there are only a few such sites.

  **Conclusion: the hypothesis is false.** The code in 0x4d4000..0x533000 was
  built by cl 13.10, the same compiler as the rest of the binary. Neither cl
  13.00 nor cl 12.00 explains the caller-first ("T") order. Getting an older
  compiler will not raise the 20-35% byte-exact rate there; the low rate comes
  from something else. Those slices should keep using vc71tk as they do now.

  **On your question about ../spore-decomp:** I checked it before downloading
  anything. It only had `vc71tk` (cl 13.10.3052, which came from
  `~/Downloads/VCToolkitSetup.exe`) and `vc9sp1` / `VCForPython27.msi` (VC9, cl
  15.00). `~/Downloads` holds the toolkit, VS2008 ISOs and GRMSDK, but no VC6 or
  VC7.0. VCToolkitSetup.exe contains only 13.10.3052. So I fetched VC6 and
  VC7.0 from archive.org. All directories under `spore-decomp/work/toolchain/`
  except `vc71tk`, `vc9sp1`, `VCForPython27.msi` and `wineprefix` are new from

  **Emission order** (`work/migrate/exp_compilers/order*.cpp`, `/O2`, with and
  without `/Gy`):
  - **cl 12.00, RTM and SP6+PP:** source order, caller before callee. This even
  holds with the 13.00 c2 from the Processor Pack.
  - **cl 13.00, 13.10.3052 and 13.10.3077:** callees first, ordered by
  call-graph depth (all leaves first).
  - **cl 13.10 flag sweep:** callee-first order stayed under every flag I tried
  with `/Og` on: `/Ob0 /Ob1 /O1 /Ox /Zi /Z7 /Gm /Oy- /GX /EHsc /Za /Gd /Gr /Gz
  /G5 /G6 /G7 /GA /Op /QIfist /GR /J /Zl /Gh /GH /GT /Gs0 /arch:SSE /Yc /FR`,
  `/TC`, EH and inline-asm callers, in-class inline members, template members,
  and TUs with 9000 functions / 5 MB of code (no size threshold).
  - **What does give caller-first order on cl 13.10:** `/Og-`, `/Od`, and calls
  that go through a vtable (no call-graph edge).

  So only VC6 reproduces the T order, but the bytes and `__ftol2` rule VC6 out.

  12.00, and no small-diff function gets closer with an older compiler. The
  slices were tuned against 13.10, which biases this, but an exact match on 377-
  or 330-byte functions is hard to fake.

  **Fingerprints in the original binary:**
  - **`__ftol2`:** VC6 calls `__ftol` (even with the Processor Pack c2), while
  13.00 and 13.10 call `__ftol2`. The image has only `__ftol2` (0x535a64),
  called 93 times from the T region and 228 times from the B region; no `__ftol`
  is linked. This alone rules out VC6.
  - **EH magic:** every FuncInfo in both regions is 0x19930520 (B 101, T-main
  23, T-small 12). VC6, 13.00 and 13.10 all emit 0x19930520 (0x19930521 started
  with VC8), so this cannot tell them apart.
  - **x87 compares:** VC6 RTM tests `fnstsw ax; test ah,1` / `test ah,0x40` for
  `<` and `==`; 13.x tests `test ah,5` / `test ah,0x44`. The binary has no `test
  ah,0x40` anywhere. The mix of 0x41 / 0x5 / 0x44 / 0x1 is about the same in
  the T and B regions.
  - **`__ehhandler` stubs:** the T-region stubs sit in the shared `.text$x` tail
  together with the B-region ones.

  **What this means for matching:** the T regime has a different cause. Untested
  candidates are per-TU `#pragma optimize` or `#pragma auto_inline`, a linker
  `/ORDER` file, or a different object/TU split (helpers in separate objects or
  COMDAT reordering). The next step would be to look at what the T helpers have
  in common (direct calls vs vtable calls, whether callers assume the callee's
  register use).

⏺ No, MinGW/GCC can be ruled out for that region:

  - Exact matches: 32 of the 93 test functions there are byte-identical to cl
    13.10's output, including complete 330- and 377-byte functions. GCC can't
    produce MSVC's exact instruction choices, register allocation and stack
    layout over that many bytes.
  - MSVC runtime: the region calls MSVC's float-to-int helper __ftol2 93 times,
    a call cl inserts itself; GCC converts inline instead. Its C++ methods pass
    this in ecx, the MSVC convention; MinGW of that era passed it on the stack.
  - Exception handling: the region uses MSVC's frame-based exception handling
    (__ehhandler stubs and FuncInfo tables with magic 0x19930520), interleaved
    with the rest of the game's. MinGW uses DWARF or setjmp/longjmp unwinding
    with different tables.
  - No GCC runtime: I searched the binary for GCC or MinGW markers (GCC: (,
    libgcc, __gxx_personality, _Unwind_*, __cxa_*, __chkstk_ms) and found none.

❯ What other C++ compilers for windows existed in that era?                     

  Thought for 12s, ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ Most C++ compilers for Windows from 2003–2008 couldn't have produced code in
  this binary at all.

  Couldn't link into an MSVC binary. Their object formats, name mangling or
  calling conventions differ, so mixing them into one link with MSVC objects
  wasn't practical:
  - Borland / CodeGear C++Builder (bcc32 5.5–5.9, OMF objects)
  - Digital Mars C++ (OMF)
  - Open Watcom 1.x (its own register calling convention)
  - Metrowerks CodeWarrior for Windows (discontinued around 2002)
  - MinGW GCC 3.x / 4.x (already ruled out)
  - LCC-Win32 and Pelles C (C only, no C++)

  MSVC-compatible: the only ones that could be in the same link:
  - Microsoft's own compilers: VC6 (12.00), VS.NET 2002 (13.00) and VS.NET 2003
    (13.10, plus its 2006 SP1 build, 13.10.6030). Other builds came with the
    Windows DDK and Platform SDK (e.g. 13.10.4035), plus VS 2005 (14.00) and VS
    2008 (15.00).
    - VC6 and 13.00 are ruled out.
    - 13.10 SP1 and the DDK build are being tested right now.
    - VS 2005/2008 are out: their code would carry their own runtime calls and
      newer exception-handling tables (magic 0x19930521/22), and the binary has
      only 0x19930520.
  - Intel C++ 7–10: the one real alternative. It was a drop-in replacement
    inside Visual Studio, with the MSVC ABI, name mangling and exception
    handling, and its objects link with MSVC's. Studios used it per project for
    hot code. But it leaves fingerprints: its helper library
    (__intel_fast_memcpy, __intel_cpu_indicator_init, libirc/libmmt, a
    "GenuineIntel" check). I just searched the binary and found none, so it's
    out.
  - Comeau C++: a niche front end that translated C++ to C and compiled that
    with MSVC. The output would be genuine MSVC code with different function
    order. It's possible in principle, but it was rare in game studios, and it
    fails on these functions anyway: the 32 byte-exact matches compiled straight
    from C++ with cl 13.10.

  So the realistic options left are another 13.10 build (being tested), or the
  same compiler with per-function pragmas, a linker order file, or a different
  file split. The investigation subagent covers all of those.
