  From me, or from you? :)                                                      

  Thought for 12s (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ That was my call, not yours. You never weighed in. "Needs a later decision"
  was my phrasing for something I flagged and deferred.

  What it is: the original game was built from some number of source files
  (translation units). In most regions M4 grouped functions into one module per
  original source file. It could do that because the binary shows where one file
  ends and the next begins: functions sit together in address order, share
  static data, and leave __FILE__ strings in asserts. In char_sheet and mission5
  those clues are missing, so the agents kept one module per slice. That gave
  28 small modules for char_sheet, while the original was probably 1–3 files.

  Why it doesn't matter yet:
  - It has no effect on correctness or byte-exactness, since every function
    compiles the same in either layout.
  - It's purely about how the source tree is organised.

  My recommendation: leave it until the byte-exactness phase. Matching work
  there will expose shared helpers, the order of static data and inlining
  patterns, and those are the boundary evidence that's missing now. Then I'd
  merge the modules into likely source files based on that evidence. If none
  turns up, I'd merge runs of neighbouring addresses so the tree isn't
  fragmented, and note that the boundaries are guesses.

  I'll do it that way unless you'd rather keep the modules split until there's
  evidence.

✻ Sautéed for 15s · done Saturday 8:34 AM

❯ "until the byte-exactness phase" ouch.                                        
                                                                                
  I'm guessing you believe "equivalent" is different, but not obviously so?     
                                                                                
  At least when it compiles we'll be able to get the populated objects that     
  will                                                                          

  Thought for 37s, ran 2 shell commands (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ Yes, mostly. "Equivalent, not exact" means the source compiles to different
  bytes but behaves the same as far as we can test. Usually the differences are
  codegen choices, not logic:
  - which registers it uses,
  - the order of instructions or basic blocks,
  - whether it uses a jump table or a chain of compares,
  - what gets spilled to the stack.

  The catch is that "as far as we can test" covers a lot of ground. equiv.py
  runs both versions under emulation on random inputs, so it's sampling, not
  proof. Here are the verdicts on the module nonmatching rows. The notes are
  free text, so these counts are approximate:

  ┌───────────────┬──────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │    Verdict    │ Rows │                What it tells you                 │
  ├───────────────┼──────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ PASS          │ ~190 │ Outputs matched and every branch was exercised.  │
  │               │      │ Strong evidence.                                 │
  ├───────────────┼──────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ WEAK          │ ~330 │ Outputs matched, but some paths were never       │
  │               │      │ reached.                                         │
  ├───────────────┼──────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │               │      │ Couldn't be run: it calls into D3D/IO/virtuals,  │
  │ UNSUPPORTED   │ ~330 │ needs structured objects, or isn't callable      │
  │               │      │ (catch funclets). No test evidence at all.       │
  ├───────────────┼──────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤

⏺ Yes, and it's the best route to stronger verdicts. One refinement: we don't
  need our build to compile and run first. The original game can provide the
  populated objects today.

  How it would work:
  1. Capture. Run the real M&B under wine/CrossOver with a small hook on target
     functions. When one is entered, dump its arguments, this, and the memory
     those pointers reach (objects, vtables, arrays, strings), a few levels
     deep. The capture is real game state: troops, meshes, scenes, script
     tables.
  2. Record the callees too. For calls we can't emulate (D3D, file IO, sound),
     log what they returned in that run. During replay, both versions get the
     same recorded answers. This is what lets most UNSUPPORTED rows run at all.
  3. Replay. Load each snapshot into equiv.py's Unicorn machine and run both the
     original and our compiled function. Compare outputs and side effects as we
     do now, using real inputs instead of random pools. Mutating the snapshots
     slightly (flip flags, change counts) then reaches nearby branches.

  What it would fix:

  ┌───────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │             Today             │              Likely after               │
  ├───────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ UNSUPPORTED because the       │ Runs on real objects, with real vtables │
  │ function needs structured     │  from the original image.               │
  │ objects or virtual calls      │                                         │
  ├───────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ UNSUPPORTED because it calls  │ Runs with recorded callee results; I    │
  │ D3D/IO                        │ expect most of these become testable.   │
  ├───────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ WEAK because random inputs    │ Real state reaches the paths actual     │
  │ never reach deep paths        │ gameplay uses. Some rare error paths    │
  │                               │ stay WEAK, and mutation helps there.    │
  └───────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────┘

  struct_mesh_equiv.py already showed this works on a single function: a
  realistic Mesh moved 0x4d1410/0x4d1880 to 0 mismatches. Snapshots generalise
  it without hand-writing a builder for each struct.

  Later, once our code links into a full exe: we can run the same recorded game
  session through both executables and diff the outcomes. That tests the whole
  program at once.

  Costs and risks:
  - The game is SteamStub-packed. We'd hook the unpacked image, which we already
    have.
  - Wine and the hook need care around threads and FPU state.
  - Snapshot size has to be capped.

  This is the first item on the post-migration tooling list. Migration is
  finished once the header consolidation lands, so this would be next. Should I
  write the design (hook mechanism, snapshot format, equiv.py integration) while
  the consolidation runs?

⏺ The design is written and committed: docs/snapshot_testing.md. Nothing is
  built yet.

  What I found while checking:
  - The game state lives mostly inside the exe. Its .data section is 143 MB,
    mostly fixed global arrays (troops, parties, items, scenes). A snapshot of
    its written pages already holds most of what a function reads, and the
    untouched pages are zeros that cost nothing to store.
  - The hook mechanism already exists, but one piece was never ported.
    tools/hybrid/build.py can plant an int3 (a one-byte breakpoint) at every
    function entry. The small runtime that catches those breakpoints (cov.c)
    exists only in spore-decomp, so that mode would fail here as it stands. The
    capture runtime would be built the same way.
  - Booting the unpacked game under CrossOver has never been tested in this 
    project. The hybrid run logs are empty, so that's the first thing to
    confirm.
  - The UNSUPPORTED rows split four ways:
    - 128 failed on unrealistic random inputs. Snapshots fix these, as long as
      the game actually runs the function.
    - 8 call imports (FMOD, D3D, file IO). Fixed once the snapshots also record
      what those calls returned.
    - 118 are problems in the test harness itself (symbol resolution, our own
      copies of constants and vtables). Snapshots don't help; this is a separate
      fix.
    - 73 aren't callable functions at all (catch handlers, cold code). They
      should be reclassified, not tested.
  - Disk is tight: 60 GB free, 94% used. The snapshot store gets a 5 GB hard
    cap.

  The plan:

  Step: 0
  What happens: Port cov.c, boot the game under CrossOver, and play a session.
  This shows which of the ~1,100 equivalent-only functions gameplay actually
  runs, which bounds the win before any capture code exists.
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Step: 1
  What happens: Capture runtime: on a hit, pause the other threads, record
  registers, the x87 state and control word, the stack and TEB, the written
  .data pages, and pages reachable from the arguments (depth- and size-capped).
   Pages are stored once by content hash. Each call's real return value is also
   recorded, as a check on the replay.
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Step: 2
  What happens: Record import results during captured calls, so FMOD and file IO

  replay faithfully. D3D's COM calls stay faked identically on both sides.
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Step: 3
  What happens: equiv.py --snapshots: replay from the real state, run callees
  for
  real, compare as today, and mutate snapshots to reach nearby branches.
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Step: 4
  What happens: Sweep the rows, rewrite their notes with the snapshot evidence,
  and reclassify the 73 non-callable rows.

  Your part: step 0 needs someone to play for 15–20 minutes — menus, the world
  map, a town, a battle, the inventory screens. That gives far better coverage
  than any script. It doesn't depend on the header consolidation, but it does
  load the machine with CrossOver, so tell me when that suits you.

  Two ways to speed it up:
  1. Run G3–G7 at the same time, each in its own git worktree. Each class name
     belongs to exactly one family, so the decisions are independent. They will
     collide in some shared files, where one header or .cpp holds classes from
     several families. I'd merge them one after another at the end and finish
     with one global gate.
  2. Make the gates cheaper. A correct header merge shouldn't change compiled
     code at all. So compare each function's compiled bytes before and after,
     which costs only a compile, and re-run equivalence only on functions whose
     bytes changed. That's the same noise check I've been using by hand. Each
     family's baseline run is also redundant, since it repeats the previous
     family's after-run. Together that saves about 45 minutes to an hour per
     family.

  Estimate: let G2 finish, since it's mid-gate (about 10:30–11:00). Then G3–G7
  run in parallel for about 3 hours, plus about an hour to merge and run the
  global gate. That means done around 2–4pm today instead of 1–7am tomorrow.

⏺ I've set it up; it starts when G2 commits.

  Changes:
  - Shared compile cache. I changed the cache key in tools/difftest/slice.py to
    use repo-relative paths, so git worktrees share compiled objects. A fresh
    worktree compiled a module in 1.2s instead of 48s. No source uses __FILE__,
    so where a tree lives can't affect its code. Main recompiles everything once
    under the new key, and the G2 agent's next compiles will be cache misses
    until then, which costs time but not correctness.
  - Cheaper gate. A new tools/difftest/codegen_dump.py fingerprints every module
    row: the function's bytes, its relocations by symbol, and its symbol name.
    A family's after-fingerprints are diffed against a single baseline, and
    equivalence is re-run only on rows whose code changed. A clean header merge
    should change none. Main and a test worktree came out identical on strat (68
    rows).
  - New workflow, ready to launch:
    - G3–G7 run at the same time, each in its own worktree on branch
      hc2/<family>.
    - "Before" results come from a separate baseline worktree, so main stays
      clean.
    - A merge agent then merges the five branches into main in order. It checks
      compiles after each merge, then runs a global gate: run_all against the
      base totals, a fingerprint diff, and a duplicate-class rescan.

  When G2 commits (a watcher is waiting for it):
  1. Stop the old workflow before G3 does anything in main.
  2. Commit the two tool changes.
  3. Create the worktrees and the baseline fingerprints and run_all totals.
  4. Launch.

  G2 is in its after-sweep now, so I'd expect it within the hour. The parallel
  run should then take about 3–4 hours, finishing mid-afternoon.

⏺ G2 has taken 1h45m so far (08:03 to 09:49). About half of that is gate
  overhead that a header merge mostly doesn't need:

  Phase: Baseline
  Time: 08:03–08:28 (25 min)
  What happened: Equivalence sweep over all 1,102 nonmatching rows. The prompt
  said to filter by touched modules; the agent ran them all. Fast, because
  results were cached.
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Phase: Editing
  Time: 08:28–09:16 (48 min)
  What happened: Merging 39 class names: the actual work.
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Phase: After-gates
  Time: 09:16–now (~33 min, roughly an hour still to go)
  What happened: The same 1,102-row sweep again, this time almost all cache
  misses. 329 rows done so far at about 14 per minute, with some functions
  taking 2½ minutes each under emulation.

  Why the after-sweep misses the cache: the equivalence cache is keyed on the
  whole compiled object file. A header edit that changes any function in a
  module therefore invalidates the cache for every function in that module,
  including ones whose code is byte-for-byte identical. So the gate re-emulates
  hundreds of functions that a header merge provably didn't touch.

  Other causes:
  - The machine is loaded (load average 26–47), and Steam's helper and
    DiskVisualizer are still taking CPU.
  - I changed the compile-cache key about 10 minutes ago, so G2's compiles since
    then are cache misses. That costs one recompile per module, which is small
    next to the emulation.

  How the new gate fixes it: it fingerprints each function's own compiled code:
  its bytes, its relocations, and anything in our object file it calls or reads.
  While writing that up I caught a gap in my first version of the fingerprint.
  A header merge typically changes inline helpers, and when one of those isn't
  inlined it gets its own copy in our object file. Equivalence then runs that
  copy, so a caller's fingerprint that covered only its own bytes would miss the
  change. I've fixed it to follow those references. Equivalence then re-runs
  only on functions whose fingerprint changed.

  I'm measuring that on G2 right now: fingerprints at G1 versus G2's current
  edits. That will show how many of the 1,102 rows G2's merge actually changed.
  I expect a small number, and I'll report it when it finishes.

⏺ G3–G7 are running in parallel with a fix I made after launch:

  - Anonymous-namespace symbols depend on the source path. The compiler names
    them with a hash of the source file's location. That made one terrain_b row
    look broken in the worktrees and would have produced false "changed" results
    for those functions.
  - Fix (9d8e136):
    - The compile cache now includes the source path for any file that reaches
      an anonymous namespace. Only terrain_b/missile.h has one.
    - The fingerprint tool ignores that hash.
  - Rollout: I added the fix to all five family branches and the baseline
    worktree, and regenerated the baseline fingerprints before any family had
    used them.
  - That terrain_b row: it still reads 77/78 inside the worktrees, because
    run_all looks up symbols by the name recorded in the manifest, which carries
    main's path. Every worktree shows the same count before and after, so the
    gates aren't affected. In main it's 78/78.
  - The 20-hour keepalive for the wine compiler session ran out, so I restarted
    it.

  G2 should commit around 11:20–11:30, and I'll stop the old workflow when it
  does. G3–G7 plus the merge are on track for about 1:30–2:30pm.

❯ ETA to playability? 🥺                                                        

  Thought for 30s, ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ It depends on which build you mean. There are two candidates, and they're far
  apart.

  1. Hybrid: the original exe with our non-exact functions swapped in. Possibly 
  today.
  - We don't need to splice in the byte-exact functions, because they're
    identical to the originals already.
  - The tooling exists: build.py --hook-manifest swaps in our compiled versions,
    and hookbisect.py finds the one that breaks a run.
  - Never tested on this project:
    - Nobody has booted M&B through it yet.
    - The 1,100 equivalent-only functions carry real risk. As I said earlier,
      about 60% have weak or no test evidence.
  - Realistic outlook:
    - A first boot attempt is possible this afternoon, once consolidation lands.
    - Getting to "plays normally with all of them swapped in" is probably a few
      days of bisecting crashes. Each bad function found that way is a real bug
      fixed.
  - This is also step 0 of the snapshot plan: boot under CrossOver, then you
    play while coverage is recorded. One play session would cover both.

  2. Drop-in exe built entirely from our source. Weeks, and I'm guessing.

  That's PLAN.md stage 5 ("Relink"), and none of it has started. Our functions
  currently compile against the original exe's addresses. A standalone exe needs
  everything the functions don't cover:
  - Global data as source: the 143 MB .data/.bss section, vtables, string
    tables, and initialised tables.
  - Object-file boundaries and link order, inferred from the original layout.
  - Static initialisers, linked with the real CRT and link 7.10 at the original
    addresses.

  My rough guess is 1–3 weeks of agent waves. Most of that would go on
  recovering the global data, which we haven't measured yet, so treat the number
  loosely.

  Recommendation: go for the hybrid as soon as consolidation lands this
  afternoon. Do you have 15–20 minutes to play when it boots?

  How it works:
  - tools/difftest/verdicts.py turns a sweep's results into
    docs/equiv_verdicts.json, plus one history point per sweep. I backfilled the
    8 full sweeps since Oct 23.
  - After a new sweep, run verdicts.py --from <sweep dir>; the next --plot picks
    it up.

  Two things the chart shows:
  - The biggest share of untested code is harness limitations, not bad inputs.
    That's 361 KB, mostly large functions the harness can't set up. Snapshots
    won't fix those; harness work will.
  - The raw sweep shows 29 FAILs. Earlier I said only 5 rows were FAIL, each
    explained. That figure came from the row notes; the default sweep counts
    more. I haven't reconciled the two yet.

  2. Other things worth tracking for an outside audience:
  - Play coverage: "of the code the game runs in a 15-minute session, X% is
    byte-exact." This comes free with the hybrid boot.
  - A per-subsystem map: byte-exact share of code size per module (AI, terrain,
    UI, script interpreter), as a grid or treemap.
  - Script interpreter opcode coverage: how many of the 2,356 opcodes are
    byte-exact or equivalent. Modders know those opcodes by name from the Module
    System.
  - Names and types recovered: the share of functions with real names, and of
    class members with real names rather than padding.
  - Milestones: boots to the menu, loads a save, finishes a battle with our code
    swapped in, drop-in exe.

  If you want to share any of this, I can also turn it into a public progress
  page.

  3. The 143 MB isn't an arena, and it isn't agents. I traced every code
  reference into .data/.bss. About 139 MB of the 144 MB is one global object at 
  0xa76630: the terrain generator.
  - Terrain::reset (0x4647e0) writes members at offsets 0xc3b0e4, 0x343b0e8,
    0x5c3b4f0 and 0x843b8f8. Those are four fixed grids of about 40 MiB each
    (0x2800000 apart), sized for the largest possible terrain.
  - Everything else in .data is small.

  This was a reasonable choice for a 2008 indie engine:
  - .bss costs nothing in the exe file.
  - Windows only commits pages when they're first touched, so the unused part of
    the grid costs no RAM.
  - It avoids heap fragmentation in a 32-bit process, and there's no lifetime to
    manage.
  - The real cost is address space: 139 MB permanently reserved out of a 2 GB
    32-bit process. That matters when big texture loads push against the 2 GB
    limit, not for RAM.

  On 2,048-character battles:
  - Agents aren't static. AgentTable is a heap-allocated vector of pages of 16
    agents, so .bss doesn't cap battle size.
  - The real walls would be:
    - per-agent CPU cost (AI, collision, x87 skeletal animation);
    - any hard caps in code, like ID widths;
    - the 32-bit address space.
  - With full source, a native 64-bit port (plan goal 2) removes the 
    address-space problem. The terrain grids could then be allocated to the
    scene's actual size.

  I haven't looked for the actual battle-size cap yet, so I can't tell you where
  1.011 stops.

  On the consolidation side, the terrain object is itself declared five
  different ways across modules (g_terrain, g_water_obj, terrain_obj, GenA, …),
  a candidate for G3's terrain family. The consolidation run is still on track
  for about 1:15–1:45pm.

✻ Churned for 6m 57s · done Saturday 12:40 PM

❯ "edges unreached" you mean instructions or branches, right?                   

  Thought for 8s (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ Branches, more precisely control-flow edges. An edge is one possible outcome
  of a jump: the taken side of a conditional, its fall-through side, or one
  target of a switch's jump table. The harness records which edges ran, on both
  the original and our version.

  Edges are stricter than instructions. In if (x) y = 1;, a single input with x
  true runs every instruction, but the edge where x is false (skipping the
  assignment) is never exercised. A bug on that path, such as an inverted
  condition, would go unseen.

  So the verdicts mean:
  - PASS: every required edge was taken in both the original and ours, and every
    output matched. The harness excludes edges that it can prove are
    unreachable.
  - WEAK: outputs matched on every input tried, but at least one edge never ran.
    The result files also record instruction coverage separately. A WEAK row
    often has 100% instruction coverage and still misses an edge.

  I'll make the chart labels say so:

  Ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ I've relabelled the chart to "PASS: matched, every branch outcome taken" and
  "WEAK: matched, some branch outcomes never taken". The docstring in
  verdicts.py now explains what an edge is (5a72e7b).

  How much work would it be to compile a 64-bit port?                           

  Thought for 16s (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ A rough answer needs a few measurements of what in the source assumes 32-bit:

  Thought for 30s, searched for 1 pattern, ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ It's a lot of work, and most of it isn't the 64-bit part. I'd estimate 4–8 
  weeks of agent waves, very roughly, plus one big prerequisite. Here is the
  breakdown from the current source (141,500 lines).

  0. Prerequisite: a standalone 32-bit build (plan stage 5). About 1–3 weeks.
  - Today our code doesn't stand alone: it calls into the original exe's globals
    by address. There are 2,115 extern declarations annotated with original
    addresses and 285 literal addresses cast to pointers, such as
    ((GenA*)0xa76630)->reset().
  - Those globals, vtables, string tables and static initializers have to become
    real source and link into a complete exe.
  - A 64-bit port can't start before this, and this stage is worth doing for its
    own sake anyway.

  1. Make the source pointer-size independent. About 1–2 weeks. This code was
  written to match 32-bit layouts byte for byte, and on x64 pointers become 8
  bytes:

  ┌───────────────────────────────┬───────┬─────────────────────────────────┐
  │          What breaks          │ Count │               Fix               │
  ├───────────────────────────────┼───────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Padding arrays sized for      │ 2,592 │ Name the members, or compute    │
  │ 4-byte pointers               │       │ padding from member types       │
  ├───────────────────────────────┼───────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Raw (char*)this + 0x… member  │   431 │ Turn into named members         │
  │ access                        │       │                                 │
  ├───────────────────────────────┼───────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Integer↔pointer casts         │  ~370 │ intptr_t / real types           │
  ├───────────────────────────────┼───────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Inline __asm blocks (x64 MSVC │    14 │ Intrinsics or plain C           │
  │  has no inline asm)           │       │                                 │
  ├───────────────────────────────┼───────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Structs written to disk as    │       │ Check that save and resource    │
  │ raw bytes                     │    ~9 │ formats serialize field by      │
  │                               │       │ field                           │
  └───────────────────────────────┴───────┴─────────────────────────────────┘

  Byte-exact matching needs the 32-bit layouts exactly, so this should be a
  separate port configuration (macros/typedefs) rather than edits that break
  matching.

  2. Replace the third-party libraries that are 32-bit only. The long pole, 
  about 2–3 weeks.
  - Newton 1.x (41 imports): no 64-bit build exists. We'd port to modern Newton
    or Jolt (the plan already mentions Jolt). The risk is behaviour changes in
    ragdolls, collisions and missiles.
  - FMOD 3 (26 imports): has no 64-bit build either. Replace it with modern
    FMOD, OpenAL or SDL3 audio. That's a thin shim, so lower risk.
  - SkinMagic (UI skinning, imported by ordinal): replace or drop.
  - D3D9 + d3dx9: 64-bit versions exist, so this is mostly fine. A macOS/Linux
    build needs a translation layer regardless.

  3. Floating point. x64 compiles floats to SSE, not x87, so results differ in
  the last bits. That's fine for single player. The visible risk is anything
  tuned to x87 precision.

  A shortcut if the goal is just memory headroom: the shipped exe isn't
  large-address-aware (flags 0x10f, bit 0x20 clear). Setting that one bit raises
  the limit from 2 GB to 4 GB on 64-bit Windows/Wine, with no port at all. The
  M&B community has used that trick on later versions. It's an hour of work, and
  we could even put it in the hybrid build.

  On 2,048-agent battles: 64-bit fixes address space, not CPU. Each agent runs
  AI, collision and skeletal animation every frame. Any hard cap in the code,
  such as ID widths, would also need finding. I haven't looked for those yet.

❯ Is the game singlethreaded or multithreaded? Does it take advantage of as     
  many CPU cores that the system has, or only up to ~4?                         

  Thought for 6s (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ Checking the binary: thread creation sites, synchronisation primitives, and
  whether it ever asks how many cores there are.

  Thought for 8s, ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ Game code doesn't call CreateThread directly—only the CRT does—so I'll trace
  how 0x4d9450, which uses GetProcessAffinityMask, an event, and a critical
  section, starts its threads via the CRT.

  Thought for 3s, searched for 1 pattern, ran 2 shell commands (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ The worker's source is elsewhere. Finding 0x4c8900:

  Thought for 22s, ran 2 shell commands (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ It's essentially dual-threaded. The game uses at most two cores of its own, 
  however many the machine has. (Libraries add threads of their own, covered
  below.)

  What the code does:
  - WinMain (0x4d9450) calls GetProcessAffinityMask. If the machine has more
    than one CPU and force_single_threading is off in rgl_config.txt, it starts
    exactly one worker thread with _beginthread, plus a critical section and an
    auto-reset event. Game code never creates another thread. The core count is
    only checked for "more than 1"; it's never used to size anything.
  - The worker (0x4c8900) only runs physics:
  while (running) {
      WaitForSingleObject(event, INFINITE);
      EnterCriticalSection(&cs);
      if (dt > 0) { g_phys.update(dt); dt = 0; }   // Newton world step
      LeaveCriticalSection(&cs);
  }
  - The main thread runs Screen::tick (0x5261e0) with that same lock held. That
    covers the whole frame of game logic: AI, agents, missions, triggers, UI. At
    the end of the tick it releases the lock and signals the event. So the
    Newton step overlaps with whatever the main thread does outside the tick,
    mainly rendering. It never overlaps with game logic.

  Threads you'd see in a profiler that aren't game code:
  - FMOD 3's mixer and streaming threads;
  - the Direct3D driver's threads;
  - under Wine, the wineserver and its helper threads.

  Newton 1.x has no multithreaded solver: the only related import is
  NewtonSetSolverModel, no thread-count call. So physics is one thread as well.

  So it scales to 2 cores, not 4. A big battle is bound by the main thread:
  per-agent AI, animation and collision queries all run in Screen::tick. A 3rd
  core and beyond sit idle. That's the real wall for large battles, more than
  memory. With full source, the obvious port targets are parallel per-agent AI
  and animation updates, plus a physics engine that uses all cores. Jolt does.

  One cleanup to note: the same global, the event at 0x5e28d8, has two names in
  our source. It's g_load_event in gui_edit (where the worker is misnamed
  loader_thread_body) and g_mt_event in cls_map, and the critical section
  likewise has two names. That's the same kind of duplication the class
  consolidation fixes, but for globals. It's a natural next pass after the
  header work.

  The class consolidation is nearly done. All five families (G3–G7) committed,
  and the merge agent has already merged them into main. It's running its final
  checks now.

  The names workflow:
  1. Decide: three agents choose one canonical name, type and header per
     address: one for the 273 globals and two for the 869 functions. They edit
     nothing. Each decision is one of:
     - rename: the names all mean the same thing;
     - member access: the "global" is really a field of a bigger object, like
       the names that point at the game object;
     - keep aliases: the linker folded identical functions into one body, so the
       names are genuinely distinct functions;
     - skip: scanner noise.
  2. Canonical: one agent writes the canonical declarations and commits. In
     shared headers it keeps the old names temporarily as marked aliases, so no
     module breaks mid-run.
  3. Apply: five agents, one per group of module directories, each in its own
     worktree. The groups don't overlap and each has about 820 declarations to
     touch.
  4. Merge: merges the branches, deletes the old aliases once nothing uses them,
     runs the global checks, and reruns the scanner for a before/after count.

  The gate that makes renames safe (5072960): a new codegen_dump.py --resolved
  mode fingerprints each external symbol by the original address it resolves to,
  not by its name. I tested it on cls_map. Renaming g_mt_event changed 0 of 117
  rows. Pointing it at the wrong address changed exactly the one function that
  uses it (WinMain). So a pure rename should show zero changed rows, and
  anything else gets explained or checked with equivalence.

  I'll launch it as soon as the merge reports, and tell you what the merge found
  first.

⏺ Explanation first, then the patch.

  "Weeks" was pessimistic, and "143 MB" was misleading. I measured it properly
  earlier and should have framed it better. Of the 143.9 MB in .data/.bss, only 
  0.2 MB has initial values. The rest is zero-filled .bss, mostly the one 139 MB
  terrain object, and zero-filled data just needs a declaration of the right
  size. The real data work is about 0.2 MB of initialised .data plus 0.39 MB of 
  .rdata: strings, constants, vtables, jump tables, initialised tables.

  What actually makes a relink take time:
  1. The exe has no relocation table. It was linked at a fixed base, so nothing
     records which dwords in the data are pointers and which are just numbers.
     We saw that already: 0x05f5e100 looks like an address but is 100,000,000.
     To turn the data into source, every pointer must become a symbol reference,
     each one found by heuristics plus our type information. This is the
     riskiest part, because a wrong guess becomes a silent bug.
  2. Our code points at original addresses. There are 285 literal addresses
     ((GenA*)0xa76630) and 2,115 extern annotations. The test harness resolves
     them by address; a real link needs real definitions behind every name. The
     names pass running now is the first step of that.
  3. Vtables. Many of our classes are partial views that call virtuals through
     raw slot offsets. The compiler only emits a correct vtable if a class
     declares its virtuals in the original order, so it's either finish those
     class definitions or carve the vtables out as data.
  4. Static initialisers. Global objects with constructors must exist as source
     definitions, and C++ runs their constructors in object-file link order. Get
     the order wrong and the game can crash before WinMain.
  5. Libraries: link the real VC7.1 libcmt/libcpmt, plus the dinput8.lib data
     formats.
  6. Then debugging it. It's the same risk as the hybrid, plus everything above.

  So my estimate is more like 1–2 weeks of agent waves, with pointer
  identification (1) and initialisation order (4) as the unknowns. The hybrid
  sidesteps all of it by borrowing the original exe's data, which is why it can
  run tonight.

  Now the build.py patch:

⏺ CONTRIBUTING.md and the setup script are written and tested. I'll commit
  everything together once the codegen.md port, still running in the background,
  comes back and I've reviewed it.

  What's done:
  - tools/setup_toolchain.py, which builds the toolchain from the installers you
    supply, checking each one by hash:
    - vctoolkit decodes VCToolkitSetup.exe's InstallShield payload (no need to
      run the installer) and extracts cl 13.10.3052, in under a second;
    - winsdk gets the SDK 6.0A headers and sal.h from VCForPython27.msi;
    - dxsdk gets the June 2010 headers, checked against their hashes;
    - wine creates the project's own wine prefix;
    - check compiles tstring and expects 33/33.

    I ran it in a throwaway directory with your installers, and the output is
    byte-identical to the toolchain the project uses. The input check stops
    wrong builds of the first two installers; the DirectX SDK is checked through
    the hashes of its extracted headers. Steps refuse to overwrite existing
    outputs.
  - CONTRIBUTING.md:
    - requirements: your own Steam copy of 1.011 (with the exe's SHA-1), wine,
      msitools, p7zip, uv, Ghidra, and the three installers with their hashes.
      It says plainly that Microsoft no longer distributes two of them and that
      we don't redistribute any;
    - setup: the commands, end to end;
    - matching loop: pick a nonmatching row, card.py, edit the module .cpp,
      chk.py, then run_all.py, plus equiv.py when it doesn't match yet. I ran
      each command as documented;
    - rules and how to submit.
  - README.md now points to CONTRIBUTING.md instead of the spore-decomp
    symlinks.

  Still pending: the docs/codegen.md port. Then I'll repoint matching.md's links
  from spore-decomp to the local copy.

  Two small things I noticed:
  - chk.py doesn't know the <stem>.manifest.txt naming, so it calls a module's
    existing manifest rows "not yet in manifest". That's harmless but confusing.
  - docs/matching.md still describes the slice-era layout
    (match/slices/<id>/...). CONTRIBUTING.md documents the module layout, and
    matching.md should catch up.

  - `#pragma float_control(precise, off)` with `(float)sqrt((double)x)` for an
  inline fsqrt. The spore guide tags it [13]/[15], but it also says VC7.1 has no
  `/fp:` switch.
  - The `/fp:fast` advice for `_CIsqrt` versus inline `fsqrt`. cl 13.10 ignores
  `/fp:fast`, so the advice is self-contradictory.
  - `(float)sqrt((double)x)` giving `fld; fsqrt` versus `sqrtf` giving the SSE
  form (§16). It reads as cl15 behaviour.

  holes), because M&B is `/O2` only.
  - All `/GS` cookie entries, including the `uint32_t pad[]` workaround and
  "/GS- ignored unless every array is uint32_t[]". The M&B build has no `/GS`; I
  did not verify whether cl 13.10 enables it by default.
  - `fabsf` handling: the `#pragma intrinsic(fabs)` trick and `<math.h>` making
  `fabsf` an intrinsic.
  - `__declspec(dllimport)` on `wcsstr`, because it assumes `/MD`.
  - The "member access versus raw offset casts is not a lever" experiment, which
  was run on cl15.
  - The min/max pointer-select entry (without addressable locals "cl emits
  cmov"). That is unlikely on an x87-only, no-`/arch` build.
  - `__assume(p == 0)` on null AutoRefCount temporaries, the hinted map insert,
  and "pass the raw pointer to the AutoRefCount copy". `__assume(0)` does appear
  in M&B sources, but none of these is shown as a codegen lever.
  - The NaN-polarity and `Vec4`/SSE items, and `/arch:SSE` flag recipes. M&B is
  x87-only.

    function and we fix it. Every such crash is a real bug in our source that
    the tests missed.
  - About 14 functions get refused for ABI reasons, like the 8 we declared void
    when the original returns a value. Those are real bugs too; I'd fix them

⏺ The trial link compiles and links everything, then fails with 3,976 distinct 
  unresolved symbols. That's the real gap list. Sorting them into categories:

  Thought for 33s, ran 2 shell commands (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ A trial link gives the exact answer. I compiled all 170 module sources (every
  one compiles) and linked them with link.exe 7.10 against the real VC7.1
  runtime (libcmt/libcpmt), the Windows import libraries and the DirectX SDK.
  The linker reports 3,976 distinct unresolved symbols and 19 duplicate 
  definitions. Sorted by cause:

  #: 1,675
  What the linker can't find: Calls to functions that do exist in our source, 
  under a different name or signature, e.g. rgl::identity(), EmitSub::emit(...)
  Why: Each module declared its callees its own way, so the decorated names
  don't
  match the definition. The test harness never noticed, because it resolves
  calls by address, not by name.
  Fix: Make every call site use the definer's declaration. The names pass
  merging
  right now fixes part of this; signature mismatches need the canonical
  headers. Mostly mechanical, gated by run_all and fingerprints.
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  #: 1,222
  What the linker can't find: Global variables declared extern but defined
  nowhere: g_items, g_iWindowWidth, …
  Why: Our code only ever declares globals, at the original's address; the
  original exe provides the storage.
  Fix: Define each one once with its real type. Most live in .bss and just need
  a
  size. The ~0.2 MB of initialised .data needs real initial values, and the
  tables of pointers in it must become symbol references. This is the hard
  part, because the exe has no relocation table.
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  #: 294
  What the linker can't find: Functions and data with no address annotation,
  e.g.
  MBStringRec::~MBStringRec, Agent::pick_slot_anim, g_tick_lo
  Why: Declared somewhere but never defined anywhere. Typically a helper the
  original inlined, or a declaration a module invented.
  Fix: Investigate each one: write the body or make it inline.
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  #: 89
  What the linker can't find: Functions at an address that has no definition in 
  src/, e.g. mnode::get_verts, Agent::duration
  Why: Probably functions the linker folded together, thunks, or bodies that
  never got a source file.
  Fix: Add the missing definitions.
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  #: 70
  What the linker can't find: Newton (41), FMOD 3 (27), SkinMagic (2)
  Why: Those DLLs ship without import libraries.
  Fix: Generate .lib files from the DLLs' export tables. About an hour.
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  #: 16
  What the linker can't find: CRT functions under the wrong declaration, e.g.
  _atol, _sprintf, mb_vsprintf
  Why: Declared without extern "C", or under custom names.
  Fix: Fix the declarations.
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  #: 19
  What the linker can't find: Duplicate definitions, e.g. AgentTable::next_used
  defined in two modules, __fltused defined in our source
  Why: Leftovers from migration.
  Fix: Keep one.

  What the linker can't show yet, all runtime issues:
  1. Pointers inside the initialised data. Strings, function tables and
     vtable-like tables must point at the right symbols. With no relocation
     table, telling a pointer from a number in that 0.2 MB of data takes our
     type information plus heuristics, and a wrong guess becomes a crash.
  2. Static constructors. Global objects' constructors must run in a valid
     order. The CRT runs them in object-file link order, so the file order
     matters.
  3. Behaviour. The same risk as the "all" hybrid: about 60% of the
     equivalent-only functions have weak or no test evidence.

  Revised estimate. Most of the 3,976 is mechanical declaration and definition
  work that agents handle well, and the names pass already covers some of it.
  I'd now say roughly a week of agent waves to a linking exe, plus however long 
  the runtime debugging takes. That's shorter than the "1–2 weeks" I gave before
  I'd measured anything.

❯ >The compiler rejects that ("destructor cannot return a value"), and the      
  agent is reverting those cases.                                               
                                                                                
  Huh? But isn't that correct...? Or how do you declare a destructor in C++?    

  Thought for 5s (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ Your syntax is right: a destructor is declared ~World();, with no return type
  and no parameters. The error means the renamed declaration had a return type.
  Checking the actual line:

  Thought for 11s, ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ You're right, and the agent's diagnosis was correct but my one-line summary
  made it sound wrong. The problem was a mechanical rename that kept a return 
  type:

  // before: a named alias for the destructor's address (scene_world.h:40)
  void destroy();                 // 0x475d50   ("old name of 
  CellGrid::~CellGrid")

  // what the alias-removal step produced: the identifier swapped, `void` kept
  void ~World();                  // C2577: destructor cannot return a value

  // what a destructor declaration has to look like
  ~World();

  Why the alias existed: 0x475d50 is the CellGrid/World destructor; the decide
  step found they're the same class. Some module called it as a plain method,
  w->destroy(). The equivalence harness resolves calls by address, so that
  declaration was enough for testing.

  What the agent did: its script replaced the name and left the rest of the line
  alone, which produced invalid C++. Reverting it to void destroy() makes the
  file compile again, but it's a stopgap. In a real link, destroy has no body,
  so it lands in the trial link's "missing body" or "no annotation" bucket.

  The proper fix: delete the alias and write the call sites as w->~World().
  That's legal C++, an explicit destructor call, and compiles to the same call
  the original makes. I'll check what the merge did with this and similar cases.
  If it reverted them, they go on the relink list, and the fingerprint gate
  will confirm the code is unchanged when they're fixed properly.

✻ Crunched for 12s · done Saturday 10:37 PM

❯ good lord lmao                                                                

  Thought for 5s (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ Yeah. The names pass has been the slowest part of the day for something that
  should have been mechanical. Two design mistakes, both mine:

  1. The old aliases hid the breakage. I kept old names alive in shared headers
     so the groups could work independently. That meant no group's gates ever
     saw the final state, so all the broken renames surfaced together at the
     end, in one tree, during the merge. Next time I'd have each group build
     once with the aliases already removed, so it catches its own breakage
     before committing.
  2. The renames were text substitution, not C++-aware. That's how void 
     destroy() became void ~World(). A rename tool that understands declarations
     (clang's AST, or even just a rule that a destructor target drops the
     return type and arguments) would have avoided most of the rounds.

  It's close now: 2 files left, then the gates.

  Thought for 5m 57s (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ Yes, you're right. The "3,270 functions, 100%" figure is functions only, and
  it leaves out two things:

  1. Globals and static data. None of the original's global variables are
     defined in our source. Modules declare them extern with an address comment,
     and nothing defines them. Right now the standalone link fills them by
     copying the original's .rdata (384 KB), initialized .data (188 KB) and the
     143 MB .bss layout into mb_data.obj, with about 1,180 labels pointing into
     it. That's borrowing from the original exe, not decompiled source. It works
     for playing the build, but turning it into real definitions (types,
     initial values, which module owns each one) is a separate job. progress.py
     doesn't measure it yet.
  2. The 82 static initializers and atexit destructors (0x5479a0–0x548570). They
     sit at the end of .text, inside the address range progress.py treats as
     static CRT/C++ library code. They're really game code (constructors of the
     game's globals), so the range boundary was wrong for them. I just wrote
     them in src/game/static_init/static_init.cpp: 71 of 82 are byte-exact so
     far, and I'm testing the other 11 for equivalence now.

  So the honest statement is: all game functions have source; the game's global 
  data does not, and the static initializers had been missed. I'll fix the
  counter so the initializers count as game code, and add a data line to the
  progress report (how many globals are defined in source versus borrowed from
  the image) so this gap shows. I'm continuing with the build while the
  equivalence check runs.

⏺ progress.py now has a "Static data" section, committed as d8043ad. It reads
  the latest snapshot that tools/relink/data_coverage.py --record writes to
  docs/data_history.json:

  Static data: 2046 of 3625 game data items come from our source (56.44%); the 
  rest the standalone link takes from the original image.
  Named globals: 44 defined in source, 789 borrowed (string literals, constants 
  and vtables are the compiler's)
  Class                   Items   Share  .rdata+.data  Share (bytes)      .bss
  defined in source          44   1.21%        5.0 KB          0.96%    0.0 MB
  generated from source    2002  55.23%      308.1 KB         59.64%    0.0 MB
  borrowed from image       789  21.77%       11.4 KB          2.20%  126.9 MB
  reached through tables    790  21.79%      192.1 KB         37.20%   16.8 MB
  library data              538       -       49.6 KB              -    0.0 MB

  The 56% is flattering: nearly all of it is string literals, float constants
  and vtables that the compiler regenerates from our code. The real gap is in
  named globals, where our source defines 44 and borrows 789.

  How it's measured: the original exe has no symbols, so data items are
  recovered from how the code uses them:
  - an item starts at each address an instruction uses, or that the resolver
    names, or that a run of 4+ pointers in the data points to (pool page
    tables);
  - an item extends to the next start, so sizes are approximate;
  - the import address table is left out.

  How to read the bytes: the .rdata+.data column is content that would have to
  be reproduced. .bss is just storage, dominated by a few huge objects; the
  terrain object at 0xa76630 alone is about 123 MB.

  "Reached through tables" means storage that no instruction addresses directly,
  only pointer tables in the data. The largest examples are the pages of the
  paged pools.

  Function count: the counter had skipped everything after the CRT, which left
  out the game's 82 static initializers and destructors. They're now in
  src/game/static_init/ (71 byte-exact, 11 equivalent), and status.py counts
  them, so the total goes from 3,270 to 3,352 game functions, still all with
  source.

  Trial-link history: the corrected point is 2,336 unresolved without the glue.
  Earlier points missed every LNK2001 error, which is why they read lower
  (1,713).

  haven't reported back. When they do, I'll merge their work, re-run the glued

  about first.

  Fix 1, the crash at 0x500045dc. The build copies the original exe's data into
  ours, and while doing so it skipped one entry in the rgl::mesh vtable (the
  table of a class's virtual functions). The entry sits right after the float
  0.01, and the combined bytes read as the text #<0wA, so glue.py treated them

  the middle of an unrelated function. A string now has to start on a 4-byte
  boundary or right after a NUL. That also fixed a second vtable with the same
  problem.

  and sphere_obj. Those were placeholder classes that only exist in our source

  body therefore reported its type as 0, which the resource manager rejects. It
  now creates the real composite and sphere, and that function (0x41b5a0) is

  16-dword block. Each cell reads two ints (ref count, tile count), not three.
  The faces section reads its count, then per face a float at +0x200, an int at
  +0x1fc and the entry count. The old 0x204-byte scratch read is gone.
  - **Pose loop:** the point block size comes from
  `lod38->meshes[0]->get70_rec()` (inline +0xa1 check, else 0x40eba0), and each
  pose then calls `ItemPage::place(i)` (0x4c6b30) on `this`. It used to call
  `copy_troop`.
  - **Columns and materials:** `cols[i]` is stored only while i < 0x40. The
  record vectors are resized with `ArrSet()`, then
  `TroopMgr::copy_troop(&recs[i], lod)` is called on `this`. The material block
  runs only when the count is non-zero, and the missing-mesh error tests
  `lod38->has`, as the original does.
  - **String tables:** the counts are stored at +0x194 / +0x198.
  - **Cells:** `vector<E176>::resize` (0x4e41e0) replaces `operator new[]`, with
  the fill value built in place by `MissionRec2()`. I reach it through a cast
  member-function pointer, because `E176` has no constructor of its own. Each
  cell now looks up both materials (name, and name + ".LOD"), stores the
  `pack_color` result back into the color field, pushes matching string-table
  indices onto the cell's `vector<int>`, and fills the tiles from r_uint +
  `unpack_color`.

  search stops at the first match. The order of the object and the three scalars
  is now get_object70, then r_float at +0x1ec, then r_int at +0x1f0 and +0x1f4.

  **Literal addresses:** only the existing `0x598328` and `0x598308` remain. The

⏺ Agent "Fix vtable slot mismatches" finished · 10m 39s

  Thought for 3m 23s (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ A subagent fixed the seven vtable-slot mismatches. Verifying and committing:

  Thought for 11s, ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ Yes, record and replay is the right next step, and I'd like to build it.
  Static checking is what got the game this far: it now loads all module data
  and reaches the main-menu loop. But the remaining fault (the logo drawn
  rotated and squeezed at the left edge, everything else black) is in render
  math that compiles cleanly and calls the right functions. Real recorded inputs
  are the way to find that kind of bug.

  How it would work
  - Capture. tools/hybrid/build.py already makes a runnable patched copy of the
    original exe (the real one is never touched) and can plant a breakpoint at
    every function entry. I'd add a --capture runtime: for the first few calls
    of each function that runs on the way to the main menu, it saves the
    registers, the stack, and the game's writable memory with all-zero pages
    dropped.
  - Replay. equiv.py already runs the original function and our compiled one
    side by side in an emulator and compares every memory write, the return
    value and the calls made. I'd add a mode that starts both from a captured
    state instead of random inputs. Any function that gives a different result
    from the same real input is a confirmed bug, with the exact field that
    differs.

  Cost and caveats
  - Build time. Most of the machinery exists. The real work is the capture
    runtime, which the coverage mode was meant to use but never brought over
    from spore-decomp (I won't touch that repo), plus the replay mode. My
    estimate is a few hours.
  - Snapshot size. It's unknown. The game process reports only 51 MB resident at
    the menu, which I doubt includes everything Wine maps. Dropping zero pages
    should keep each snapshot manageable, but I'll measure on the first capture.
  - Coverage gaps. A function that calls into Direct3D or FMOD can only be
    compared up to that call, because the emulator doesn't model them. The
    render-math helpers that most likely hold this bug mostly don't make such
    calls.

❯ What do you think then- thread/address sanitizer?                             

  Thought for 7m 9s (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ Short answer: I don't think sanitizers would pay off here.

  - ThreadSanitizer doesn't exist for 32-bit Windows targets, and the game has
    very few threads (main, sound, Wine's D3D thread). None of the bugs so far
    has been a race.
  - AddressSanitizer would mean compiling with clang-cl instead of cl 13.10. Our
    objects are tied to that compiler: VC7.1's STL layouts and name mangling,
    the /MT CRT, and exact struct layouts that the glue's copied data depends
    on. Getting the whole tree through clang-cl with VC7.1's 2003-era headers,
    then running ASan's 32-bit runtime under Wine, would be days of work with
    uncertain results.
  - Most of what we've hit isn't memory unsafety. It's semantics that differ
    from the original:
    - layouts that are off;
    - reads with the wrong number type;
    - wrong loop counts;
    - calls to the wrong virtual slot;
    - calling-convention mismatches.

    The code reads and writes valid memory, just the wrong fields. ASan only
    catches the minority that run off a buffer, and those already crash, which
    crashrun reports with a stack.

  The capture/replay oracle covers the same ground, and more of it. It sees any
  difference from the original, not just out-of-bounds accesses. If we want
  sanitizer-like checks too, they're cheap to add to the replay, since it
  already tracks every write. For example: flag a write that lands outside every
  page the original function touched, or a read of memory the original never
  reads.

  Right now, the armed capture writes its first snapshot and then the game sits
  at 0% CPU, which looks like a deadlock in my runtime. I've attached the
  debugger to dump every thread's stack after the trigger, and I'll fix the
  runtime once I see where they're stuck.

  Cause: The original links with a 4 MB stack; ours had the default 1 MB
  Fix: /STACK:0x3e8480

  Calling conventions (two names for one function, each using a different 
  convention)

  - psys_record::read: the original is cdecl (stream, record); ours was a member
    function. The skybox reader wrote floats through a garbage pointer.
  - MapSceneRec::read: takes one argument (the stream); ours took two and read
    the stream from the wrong slot. A subagent rewrote the whole function
    against the original's machine code.
  - rotate_2x2: the original is a member function, ours was a cdecl free
    function.
  - String-table lookup wrapper: cdecl, standing in for a member function.
  - SkinDialog: stdcall, one declaration said cdecl.
  - audio_close / FSOUND_Close: first resolved to a copy constructor; later a
    stray // @ 0x4dc030 marker rebound FSOUND_Close to it again.
  - Quest titles in note_window: a fake strip_tags(quest, 0) stood in for the
    real "title of quest N, markup stripped".
  - Block::read (item kinds): the original takes the file version as a second
    argument; ours tested a string field instead, so items' triggers were never
    read.

  Struct layouts

  - LoadingMeshes: pad0[0xfb0] before members commented +0x1210, so corner mesh
    pointers overwrote a mesh built at +0xfb0.
  - Block (item kinds): every field 4 bytes late, and an 8-byte gap was missing.
  - loaded_snd_table: count, records and used-list at +0/+4/+8; the original has
    +8/+0xc/+0x50.
  - ground_spec: bare padding, so new[] never constructed its name string.

⏺ The replay wasn't broken, it was just very slow: it mapped the snapshot's
  102,728 memory pages one at a time, and that cost grows quadratically. I
  changed it to map runs of adjacent pages in one call, and replaying one side
  of a snapshot dropped from over 90 seconds to 0.5 seconds. The 31 GB VS Code
  extension made things worse on top of that.

  The full replay of the 77 main-menu snapshots is running now, capped at 20
  minutes, and results are coming in:

⏺ I found and fixed a second bug in the replay tool. Every function shares one
  emulator, and each new runner loads its code at the same address. So a runner
  reused later was actually running whichever function had been loaded last.
  That caused most of the faults in the first full pass, where our side crashed
  at 0x3000xxxx on the second hit of a function. Each function now gets a fresh
  emulator, and the rerun is about 15 of 77 snapshots in.

  the first pass (487b00) turns out to be a false alarm. It's the UTF-8
  decoder, which uses a nonstandard register convention, so replaying it with
  the original's registers says nothing about our version. I'll go through the
  remaining differences once the rerun finishes.

⏺ I found a real rendering bug, the first one the capture-and-replay tool has
  caught.

  The bug: MissionUi::render (0x488720) builds the matrix used to draw every UI
  widget. Our version wrote the widget's position into the matrix's rotation
  rows, and the leftover values past the end of the matrix. So every widget was
  drawn with a corrupted rotation and a zero position. That fits the rotated,
  squeezed logo stuck at the left edge, and the missing buttons and background.
  The fix is in src/game/ui/mission_ui.cpp, and replaying both captured calls
  now gives the same result as the original. Byte-exactness hasn't been
  re-checked.

  The other differences in the main-menu snapshots came from the replay tool,
  not the game:
  - decode_utf8 uses a nonstandard register convention, so replaying it with the
    original's registers can't be compared.
  - add_quad and weather::update write into their own argument slots, which the
    replay wrongly counts as changes to the caller's memory.
  - pick returns nothing, so its eax mismatch doesn't matter.
  - The build_row trap is most likely a link alias the replay doesn't follow.

  The standalone exe is rebuilding now. Once it's done I'll launch it and
  screenshot the main menu to see whether the fix shows up on screen.

⏺ The main menu now draws correctly apart from the buttons, and that came from
  the first real bug the capture-and-replay tool caught.

  The bug: MissionUi::render builds the matrix that places every UI element on
  screen. Our version wrote the element's position into the rotation part of the
  matrix. It also wrote the remaining values past the end of the matrix and
  left the position empty. As a result everything was drawn at the origin with a
  distorted rotation, which is why the logo appeared squeezed at the left edge.
  After the fix, both captured calls replay the same as the original, and the
  rebuilt exe shows the parchment background, the Mount&Blade logo and the
  horseman in place (screenshot sent).

  What's still wrong: the menu button text isn't drawn.

  Replay tool fixes, all part of the commit:
  - Speed: replaying one snapshot went from over 90 seconds to 0.5 seconds. It
    was mapping about 100,000 memory pages one at a time; it now maps runs of
    adjacent pages together.
  - Wrong code being run: all functions shared one emulator. A function replayed
    a second time could run whichever function had been loaded last. Each
    function now gets its own.
  - Capture changes: the capture tool's --arm start trigger and direct page
    writes are committed too.

  Everything is committed as a4d1ac0, not pushed. One thing left unfixed: the
  replay still flags writes to a function's own argument slots as differences.
  They were the only differences in two of the functions (add_quad,
  weather::update).

❯ I meant can you click the "Play game" button or not from the game launcher    

  Thought for 4s (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺ Yes. Every run presses it automatically: the scripts bring the launcher to the
  front and press Return, which triggers Play. They keep doing that until
  rgl_log.txt starts growing, which means the game itself has started.

  It isn't 100% reliable, though. If another window grabs focus at the wrong
  moment, the keypress goes to that window instead. That's the likely cause of
  the two false "no menu" results earlier, and why the bisection now retries
  those runs.

✻ Crunched for 5s · done 8:12 PM

❯ Does your script work off of screenshots, or how does it know when we see the 
  text on-screen?                                                               

⏺ Yes, it works off screenshots, and it decides automatically whether text is
  visible. textcheck.py works like this:

  1. Launch the exe, press Play, and wait until rgl_log.txt says "Finished
     All...". That means loading is done and the menu is being built.
  2. Wait 8 more seconds for the menu's first frames.
  3. Capture just the game window with winshot.py. That uses macOS's own window
     capture, so it works even if other windows are on top.
  4. Count dark pixels in the area where the buttons sit (38–80% across, 30–88%
     down). The button text is dark on light parchment, and the parchment alone
     has almost no dark pixels there.

  From the calibration:
  - The original, with text, scored 0.0244 (about 2.4% dark pixels).
  - Our build, without text, scored 0.0000.

  Anything above 0.004 counts as TEXT. Every run's screenshot is kept
  (work/hybrid/tb3_N.png), so I can open any of them to confirm the call by eye.
